speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before motions are proceeded with, and in view of the discussion we had yesterday, I should like to make a suggestion to the house. I have before me a motion moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) which was passed on March 12 and referred to yesterday. This reads as follows:
For a copy of all communications that passed between veterinary officials either provincial or federal and the federal Department of Agriculture, together with all records since the 17th day of November, 1951, relative to the cattle epidemic of vesicular stomatitis or foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan, also all certificates or statements of analysis showing the results of the chemical examination of suspected specimens of either of said cattle diseases.
I should like to say to the house, through you, Mr. Speaker, that the first part of the motion, "for a copy of all communications that passed between veterinary officials either provincial or federal and the federal Department of Agriculture", cannot be acceded to because I have not been able to find any such documents on the record. Then the motion goes on:
. . . together with all records since the 17th day of November, 1951, relative to the cattle epidemic of vesicular stomatitis or foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan . . .
There is some doubt in my mind as to whether there is very much in the way of records in connection with this matter. There are on the files of the department, either here or at Regina, but mostly here, communications between the officials of the department. That is to say, one official would say to another, "we are doing so and so," and suggest to him 55704-107
what he should do. I submit that that kind of record has always been considered to be privileged, provided that the minister desires it should be privileged. This has been the general practice, and I think one can easily understand why it should be so. I am not going to refer to Beauchesne or Bourinot in connection with the matter, further than to say it is indicated in many places that unless that were the general rule it would be difficult to carry on government as a government should be carried on. I quite agree with that.
That has been the general practice. As a matter of fact, shortly after I came into this house no less a parliamentarian than the late Lord Bennett gave me a lecture on it which I have never forgotten. I think it has been generally admitted that kind of thing is privileged.
I realize that this is a rather unusual situation in that everybody has been more or less stirred up over the fighting of foot-and-mouth disease and is naturally interested in it. If the house agrees, I am quite prepared to table what is looked upon as privileged- that is, to table all the communications which are on the file. There is nothing in any of them that the government need be concerned about making available. They are the usual communications that pass back and forth between officials when they are administering anything in any department. I am quite prepared to table them all, but I should like to suggest to the house that it might approve a motion which I should like to move without notice. I know that the rules of the house require that I give two days' notice.
To alter the order, I presume.
Not to alter the order at all. I am prepared to accept the order in spite of the fact that it is poorly drawn.
It was drawn well enough to cause the minister trouble.

I now move:
That the subject of the prevalence of foot-and mouth disease in the province of Saskatchewan and its attendant ramifications be referred immediately to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.
A nice cover-up.

Again I say that I know I require the unanimous consent of the house. If I have not unanimous consent, then I should

I think it should be recognized by the house that the officials of the department have some interest in this kind of thing. It is all very well to say that we in the house have an interest in it. We have, but men who have made their lifework the work of a department have some interest in it too. Because of the discussions that have taken place here, I assume that the meetings of the standing committee on agriculture are going to be more or less of a trial of the individuals responsible for the administration of the health of animals branch of the Department of Agriculture. In fairness to these men I think I should not place on the table of the house documents which will be a part of the evidence-practically all the evidence that will be produced -before the country and put the officials in a position where they will have to wait three or four days or a week and listen to the discussion of these documents throughout the country and see it in the press without their having any opportunity to be heard.
I think it would be helpful if we could permit this matter to be dealt with immediately by the committee. The committee is meeting tomorrow morning. It was being called to consider the wheat board report and to organize for that purpose. Instead of doing that it can occupy its time by going immediately into this question. My suggestion is that by unanimous consent the house should agree to the committee going immediately into a discussion of the question tomorrow, with the knowledge that I am quite prepared to put all the documents on the table of the house, whether privileged or otherwise, and leave them in the hands of hon. members.

May I ask the minister a question? Perhaps I should address the Minister of Justice. Do these documents include the report I asked for yesterday, namely, the report made by "F" division, C.I.B., Regina town station, Royal Canadian Mounted Police, dated March 20, 1952, with respect to the Animal Contagious Diseases Act?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Replying to my hon. friend's question, I may say that in the administration of the mounted police we cannot permit the production of confidential police reports of this kind. If we do, we destroy the whole value of securing them, for reasons which I explained yesterday.
I understand there is no security involved in this case.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The position is that when police reports are prepared upon any matter at all they are prepared upon the assumption that they are confidential and are not going to be produced anywhere. A lot of information is put in them on that basis that would under no circumstances be put into a document which was not prepared with that in view. Therefore for many years the department has resisted the production of such documents, and we must continue to do so. For that matter I do not think they would' shed a great deal of light upon the question in any event, because what should be concerned here is largely a matter of people speaking about animal diseases who are qualified experts in that field.

I understand the report
discusses the quarantine and the manner in which it was carried out. It seems to me that is of as much importance to the committee as any other document.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With respect to the last point raised by my hon. friend, if he is concerned about establishing the facts as to the quarantine there is no reason why he cannot establish them by having the policemen called who were in charge of establishing the quarantine and having them give their evidence orally to the committee. That would be much more satisfactory than reading a report with speculation and the like in it.

To
begin with, I want to say that the minister's explanation today is merely an exculpatory method of refusing to carry out the will of the house.
Oh, oh.

An order was passed by the house on March 12 with the minister's consent and approval. Time has gone by. On April 7 an inquiry was made about the matter, and the same course of procrastination and postponement was followed then. The minister now says: I will comply in my own way with the order of parliament. That is an added affront to parliament. No one can atone for his failure to give the full record to parliament by simply saying: I am not going to do it in the way parliament orders; I have my own alternative which I now offer.
There is no alternative.

This matter is a serious one. Unless members of parliament can rely on records being brought down when parliament so orders; unless parliament can rely on the fact that the records possessed by the departments will not be selectively reviewed,
1683,

with the ones that can cause no difficulty being produced and the rest concealed, then an order of parliament means nothing.
Yesterday the minister made this unusual statement, as found at page 1649 of Hansard. He said:
There are some documents-as a matter of fact, I did not know this one was in existence and I do not know how the hon. member found out about it. The only document that was mentioned is the one which I think the government official who sent the message should be in a position to deal with.
I ask that the minister table these records in parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He said he would.
I ask that he do not make them subject to what a committee may decide or consider proper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He has; offered to table them right away.

I ask that they be tabled in the house. That is the only way for the house to be satisfied that the order has been carried out. I hope that what took place yesterday will not be repeated. As to consenting to proceeding with the motion the minister has introduced, my personal submission is that I can see no reason for the house to give such consent. There is only one way in which to comply with an order of the house, and that is to table the record. What I requested yesterday was that the record and documents the minister has should be tabled. That was voted down when I tried to secure action on the part of the government. It was then that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) might very well have risen and said to his minister: Produce the documents.
I ask that these documents be tabled now, and that no subterfuge be adopted whereby parliament must submit to a committee the right to say what parliament shall have.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In view of the hon. member's intimation as to what I should have done yesterday, may I remind him that the request he made yesterday was that Mr. Speaker make an order in the exercise of his powers. Mr. Speaker decided that he had no power to make such an order, that it could be made only by the house itself. It was against that decision that an appeal was taken and a vote registered, not at all upon the question whether any special document should have been laid on the table.
The hon. member does not appear to have been any more attentive to what was being said today than he was to what took place yesterday, because today the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that in spite 55704-107J
Foot-and-mouth disease-Documents of the fact that in his view it was not usual to table certain of these documents, he was quite prepared to lay the whole file on the. table. He merely added that because of the; understanding from the very first day this house met that this matter would be referred to the select committee on agriculture, he proposed doing today what in my experience has always been done and what was done no later than yesterday, when by leave of the house there was a motion by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to refer to a committee the reports he had tabled.
These are not reports.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is something which in my experience is current practice; but if there is objection to its being done without notice, the hon. gentleman or any other hon. gentleman has only to say he objects and it cannot be done without notice. Then notice will be placed in Votes and Proceedings and the motion will be called when the forty-eight hours have expired.
There have been complaints within the last few days because this matter has not yet got to the committee on agriculture, but apparently when a move is made to have it brought before the committee a technical objection is raised. It is the right of any hon. member to raise such an objection if he. thinks the public interest or any other interest will be served thereby, and I am-sure His Honour would not put this motion until he had satisfied himself there was no such objection.

May I ask one question to get this clear in my mind? I understand that the minister now proposes to do what he refused to do yesterday, namely, table the documents in question, but that he is making that conditional upon the house accepting the motion to refer the matter to the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

The Prime Minister says
that is not so. What does the minister say?.

I thought I made it very plain that if it is the wish of the house, as I understand it is, I am quite prepared to table all the documents, but I want to go on record as saying that I am tabling documents which are usually privileged in this house. In other words I do not want to be presumed to be committing anyone in future to what I am doing on this occasion. I am quite prepared to lay on the table of the house all the documents that by any stretch of the imagination can be brought under this motion.

Oh, oh.

Foot-and-mouth disease-Documents
I am prepared to lay on the table all those I think ought to be there and all those anybody else might think should be there.
Oh, oh.
Just wait until I get through. I am prepared to lay on the table all those anybody might think should be there, and there are no others in the record. They will all be laid on the table.
May I suggest to the minister that he table the documents and then move his motion referring the matter to the committee, because apparently there is confusion in the house.

There is one thing I would like to impress upon everyone here; whether or not it has any effect upon the hon. member for Lake Centre I must say it anyway. Yesterday the worst case of foot-and-mouth disease we have yet had broke out. We should not have officials who should be out fighting this disease down here before a committee any longer than is necessary, and I think it is most important that these proceedings be started tomorrow. I am not making that as a condition in connection with the tabling of the documents; I am prepared to table all the documents unless the house should say I must not do so in order to protect something or other. I am quite prepared to table them.
Table them.
All right. My hon. friend says I refused to table them yesterday. I did not refuse to table them yesterday.
Oh, oh.

Let us get this thing straight. A little laughing is not going to help it any; this is not a laughing matter. I said yesterday that these documents would be available at what I thought was the proper time. Perhaps it was not the proper thing to say but I said they would be available. The only thing I have in mind is that civil servants ought to have some rights in connection with a matter of this kind. I am not going to try to be the defender of the civil servants in connection with this matter. I am going to listen to their evidence, and I presume every member of that committee will do the same thing. Then when they have heard all the evidence they will make up their minds. But I am sure the hon. member for Lake Centre will agree that there never has been a case brought before any court in which it has been a good thing to prepare the public for a decision in a certain direction before the evidence has been heard.
I think we should start in tomorrow morning hearing the evidence. I am not making

that a condition, but I believe it should be done. If the house will not agree to that, then I ask-I said this before, but I want to repeat it-that what I have said today be considered as notice so the question may be brought up forty-eight hours hence. I repeat that I do not think forty-eight hours should be taken up in that way. Already, I have had to order one of the officials who should be out in Saskatchewan to remain here so he would be available any time this matter came up, in order that hon. members might question him. I think we should expedite that hearing as much as possible, and that is the only idea I have in mind. We have nothing to be concerned about in connection with this, any more than any other members of the house. For that reason I am quite prepared to lay these documents o.n the table; and I now do so. You can deal with them as you see fit, but I still think we should have the committee meet tomorrow.
I now move:
That the subject of the prevalence of foot-and-mouth disease in the province of Saskatchewan and its attendant ramifications be referred immediately to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.

Mr. Speaker, the minister having properly and graciously complied with the order of the house, certainly that is all we want. Let me say to the Prime Minister, however, in reply to his gratuitous remark as to whether the public interest or any other interest is served, that the interest of parliament must be served; and that was the purpose of bringing up this matter on a question of privilege.

The house has heard the motion. Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
Motion (Mr. Gardiner) agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved:
speechtext:
That a select committee be appointed to consider a bill respecting allowances for war veterans and their dependents, and to consider such other matters relating to veterans affairs that may be referred to the committee; with power to send for persons, papers and records; to print its proceedings, and report from time to time to the house; that the provisions of section 1, standing order 65, be waived in respect to this committee; and that the said committee shall consist of the following members:	Messrs. Balcer, Balcom, Bennett, Blair,
Brooks, Carter, Corry, Croll, Cruickshank, Dickey, George, Gillis, Green, Harkness, Herridge, Hosking, Jutras, Langlois (Gaspe), Larson, Lennard, Mac-Dougall, McWilliam, Mott, Mutch, Quelch, Roberge, Ross (Souris), Thomas, Tremblay, Weaver, White (Hastings-Peterborough).
Is the minister going to give us an explanation?

I hardly think this resolution calls tor any lengthy explanation. It is the usual resolution setting up a committee to study the legislation which will be introduced following the other resolutions now on the order paper.

I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am extremely pleased that the minister is setting up this committee. The only regret is that it was not set up sooner. I understand that there is a rush now to get through these resolutions before the house so that we may set up the committee and hear the views of the veterans within the next few days. This rush is just a further argument for a standing committee of this house on veterans affairs. This is a matter which has been brought before the house on a number of occasions, not only by me but by other members as well.
I do not think there is any more important subject with which this house has to deal than that of veterans affairs. There are quite a number of standing committees, and many of them never sit at all. Year after year they are set up and simply exist on paper, but the veterans affairs committee is one that could and should sit every year. Since 1935 when I came to this house we have had almost yearly veterans affairs committees. We had a committee last year, one in 1948, one in 1945, and one in 1946. This is an indication that the veterans affairs committee should be set up as a permanent institution of this house.
As I said a moment ago, veterans affairs are most important and are becoming increasingly important. After the first war we had only the first war veterans with which to deal. Today we have the veterans of the second world war, and we shall have the veterans from the Korean war. It is difficult to estimate how many veterans we may have in the future. A standing committee on veterans affairs has also been urged by all the veterans organizations across this country. They have made their recommendations to the cabinet. Therefore I ask that this matter be given favourable consideration by the government.
We may think that we have veterans affairs fairly well settled, but the changing conditions in the cost of living and in the manner of living in this country make changes necessary in this type of legislation. Just a few days ago I noticed that in the maritime provinces the officials of the Veterans Land Act were meeting. They were very much concerned over the fact that many of the young men who had been placed on the farms were
Committee on Veterans Affairs now leaving them. They found it impossible to carry on under the regulations which had been issued. I do not see any mention of that matter in any of the resolutions which are on the order paper today.
I might refer also to the number of members on this committee. Today it is thirty-one, the same as last year when we criticized the small number on the committee. In 1945, for instance, there were sixty members of that committee; in 1948 the smallest committee we had was thirty-five. There are a large number of veterans in this house, and I think we could easily increase the number on that committee. I am not going to press the point, Mr. Speaker, because it is not as important as the setting up of a permanent committee on veterans affairs, nor is it as important as another matter to which I should like to refer for a few minutes.
The terms of reference of a committee are, of course, the most important part of the resolution setting up the committee. We may ask ourselves whether our present terms of reference are broad enough. In my opinion they are not. The terms of reference in 1945 and 1946 were entirely different from those which we had in 1951, and different from the terms of reference which we have before us today. In 1945 we were permitted to consider all the legislation passed since the commencement of the war with Germany with regard to pensions, treatment, re-establishment, hospitalization, and so on. The committee was given very broad scope. In 1946 the terms were broad enough to consider nearly all veterans questions. Last year and this year, in my opinion, the terms of reference have been very narrow. For instance, in 1951 we considered them so narrow we tried to have them amended in the house to include the War Veterans Allowance Act. This motion was voted down, but repeatedly in the sessions of the committee we asked that this matter be referred back to the house so that the terms of reference might be broadened to include what we considered the most important matters concerning veterans.
I consider that last year the committee's hands were tied, and the results indicated that our terms were not broad enough to consider the matters which we all agreed should have been considered. I really think it is not unfair to say that last year the committee was an abortive committee, and that it did very little that was of benefit to the veteran. Some good matters came before the committee. For instance, the widows receive the full orphan rate for children. There is an allowance for children, continued up to the age of 21, where they are making educational progress. But these were not the broad

Committee on Veterans Affairs matters which the veterans across the country-wished to have considered. The two important matters which should have been before that committee last year were an increase in the basic rate of pension and an increase in the war veterans allowance. Most of the time of the committee last year was taken up not in considering matters which were referred to the committee but rather in considering matters which were not, but which we considered should have been, before the committee at that time.
Time and time again veterans organizations appearing before the committee emphasized the fact that they considered that the reference was too narrow and that these two important matters, namely, the basic rate of pension and the war veterans allowance, should have been before the committee for discussion.
I might say that one good result of the committee's work was that the opposition members and the veterans organizations across Canada put up such a strong argument for an increase in the basic rate of pension that at the fall session last year this matter was considered-
Oh, oh.

-and it had to be considered) 'by the government. At that time an increase was made in the basic rate of pension. But the other matter which also should have been considered at that time, the war veterans allowance, was not considered. The veterans had to wait many months for an increase in the basic rate of pension-
By-election.

-and now they have had to - wait almost a year for an increase in the war veterans allowance. My hon. friend can have the opportunity to speak, If he wishes to do so; and if there is anything I say which the facts will not bear out, I should like the hon. member to get up and point it out. He cannot do it.
As I say, the war veterans allowance should have been considered. For nearly a year, hardship has -been forced upon the old veterans of this country. They were made to wait another year. They were made to wait during a time when the cost of living was continually increasing. There has been considerable suffering. I will venture to say that there is not a member of this house who has not received many letters from war veterans across Canada pointing out the suffering and the injustice to which they have been subjected over this last year, because,


as I say, we were not allowed to consider this most important matter in the veterans affairs committee a year ago.
These letters speak about the reduction in the war veterans allowance, for instance, and count on an increase in the pension. When we put through in this house legislation giving old age security allowances to men and women to whom it was not financially necessary to give assistance, these war veterans-a segment of our population which needed assistance perhaps more than did any other people in this country-were denied this right.
As I have pointed out, Mr. Speaker, there are two matters which should have received more consideration from this house in connection with veterans affairs. One is the question of setting up a permanent standing committee on veterans affairs which could take up yearly these matters which, of necessity, must come before it. The second is the broadening of our terms of reference so that when veterans matters arise we as a veterans affairs committee will be in a position to deal with them.
I do not intend, sir, to labour this matter any further. In view of the fact that the terms of reference are again, in my opinion, too narrow to include, for instance, this matter of the Veterans Land Act and other matters I could mention, I should like to move the following amendment:
That the resolution be amended by striking out the word "such" in the third line and substituting the word "any," and in the fourth line striking out the words "that may be referred to the committee."
The resolution would then read as follows:
That a select committee be appointed to consider a bill respecting allowances for war veterans and their dependents, and to consider any other matters relating to veterans affairs, with power to send for persons, papers and records;-
And so on. The rest of the resolution is the same as it appears on the order paper.

There is a rule to the effect that the powers of a committee cannot be enlarged by an amendment. I ruled on this point before. The pertinent section of Beauchesne's third edition is citation 546, the second paragraph of which reads in part as follows:
When the house is considering a motion, of which notice has been given, for the appointment of a select committee, a member cannot move in amendment that the committee be given wider powers than those which were set down in the notice.
I would think this amendment gives the committee considerably wider powers than those which are set down in the notice. Accordingly, I cannot allow the amendment to stand.
Possibly the minister would accept the amendment.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, I think what has just taken place in the house points up the necessity for a standing committee on veterans affairs. We in the opposition try to get references to these committees widened in order to deal with matters which are constantly being brought up in our constituencies and in the country generally, but the government, by the terms of reference to the committee, limit our ability to represent the people who really want to have their cases put before the house.
We in this house passed a veterans charter. It was fairly broad in its terms, and was a reasonably good act, but to say it was a reasonably good act does not mean that it cannot be improved upon. It does not mean that difficulties in administration do not necessarily arise from time to time. With regard to the regulations under the veterans charter, the Veterans Land Act and various other acts, I am sure that hon. members on the government side have had brought to them problems which indicate that there is need for constant supervision, revision and scrutiny of those acts and of the regulations made thereunder.
After all, when we enact a law it is fairly general in its provisions; it is the administration of the act, and the regulations which are passed under it, which make it either effective or ineffective. We have had reasonably good administration; nevertheless hon. members who are going out to their constituents between sessions, meeting them and discussing their problems with them, have a better idea than any other group of how these regulations are affecting veterans in the different parts of the country. Therefore there should be a permanent veterans affairs committee of the house.
I have a resolution on the order paper to that effect. It is No. 11 on today's order paper, and reads:
The following proposed resolution: That standing order 63 be amended by inserting therein immediately after subsection (1) the following new subsection:
(m) On veterans affairs, to consist of 35 members, 10 of whom shall constitute a quorum.
Unfortunately, private members' days are being curtailed from now on, and we shall not reach this resolution on the order paper. The motion which is now before the house to set up this committee points out the necessity of a permanent committee, because at least in every second session of parliament
Committee on Veterans Affairs we have to set up a veterans affairs committee to deal with these things. Why not have a permanent committee to which could be sent references wide enough to deal with all the veterans problems that are constantly being brought before us?
I do not want to go into the details of this matter at this time, because there are various resolutions on the order paper having to do with the amendments which the government is proposing at this session. The amendments which are to be brought in under these resolutions may be good, or they may not. We have not a copy of the legislation yet. Unfortunately the legislation will be confined to certain specific amendments of specific acts. We shall not be able to deal with the other acts in the veterans affairs committee. I would urge the minister and the government to give serious consideration to setting up a permanent committee of the house to deal with veterans matters so that year by year, as we meet here in parliament, the committee can be called together, and we, as veterans of the house, can get together to discuss these problems and improve the veterans charter which the government, rightly, I think, was quite proud of when it was adopted. Surely the government should be prepared to do that; surely it should be prepared to give an opportunity to hon. members to place the problems of their constituents and the veterans in their constituencies before the committee regularly, and to suggest amendments that should be made to keep our veterans charter up to date.

Mr. Speaker, we in this group are glad to support the resolution to set up a special committee to consider amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. But we also regret that the terms of reference have not been widened sufficiently to make it possible for that committee to deal with any matter that it may consider it should be allowed to deal with. In spite of the way in which the resolution is worded, I hope that the government will see fit to allow discussion on any matter that the committee may consider should be discussed.
For instance, we all know now that last year, as a result of the curtailing of the terms of reference to exclude any discussion of the War Veterans Allowance Act, a lot of hard feeling was caused in that committee; not only hard feeling in that committee but hard feeling in the various veterans organizations throughout the dominion. As a result, last year we did not have the same degree of harmony in the committee as was usually prevalent in former committees.

Committee on Veterans Affairs
I do not want this to be interpreted as a criticism of the way in which the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch), conducted the hearings. I have always had a very high appreciation of the way in which that hon. member has acted in his capacity as chairman of the committee. I have always felt that that hon. member has a very keen desire to do everything in his power to advance the interests of this country.
I do think that the government should give consideration to making the veterans committee a permanent standing committee of this house, and that it should adopt the practice of referring to that committee the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs in exactly the same way that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) refers the estimates of his department to the external affairs committee. Such action would make it possible for us to keep up to date on the operations of the various functions of his department, and it would also help to expedite the passing of his estimates.
This is a large department; it handles a great deal of money, and it is very hard for hon. members to keep up to date on the various activities of the department. In view of the fact that this is only a special committee, and not an annual committee, I hope that the minister will, this year at any rate, when the briefs of the Legion and of other organizations are presented before it, allow a full discussion on any matter that is brought up that the committee feels should be discussed in full; otherwise a lot of bitterness will be engendered in the committee, in exactly the same way as happened last year.

I should like to add my voice to that of those advocating that there be a permanent veterans affairs committee, and that the committee meet annually to consider the affairs of veterans of this country. May I remind hon. members that if it had not been for the veterans of 1812, 1898, 1914 and 1939 there would be no houses of parliament sitting at Ottawa today. The veterans of the recent war and of previous wars have defended this country and this parliament against aggressors with mighty armies who were determined to stop this parliament from functioning.
When certain Liberal members of this house interrupt a veteran of the 1914-18 war who is pleading on behalf of the veterans of Canada, I think it is a disgrace. I think it is a disgrace for any man to interrupt a plea on behalf of a veteran or of any group of veterans.

The veterans affairs committee should be a permanent standing committee; it should be available at any time to meet the demands, requests and considerations that are made necessary by the changes that occur from time to time. Today we have advertisements prominently displayed in newspapers and various weeklies across this country asking the young men to join the air force, join the infantry, join the navy. What we are really saying to these men is this: Offer your lives, offer your arms, offer your health; offer yourself to become permanently disabled in the defence of your people and of this country. That is what we are asking these men to do, and it certainly does not behoove any member of this House of Commons to speak flippantly or to interrupt a veteran who is pleading on behalf of veterans.
There is a war on today, and it is not the last war. Hon. members know that in their hearts. The number of veterans is increasing, and their demands are increasing. It will be an honour for any man to sit on that committee, a great honour to serve to the best of his ability, to be fair and just to the men who have given their all in defence of this parliament and in defence of the people of Canada.

I wish to concur in the remarks made by the previous speakers. I regret that the minister indicated so readily that he would not agree to or approve of any extension of the terms of reference. If that is an indication that we are going to have the same type and kind of veterans affairs committee that we had in the first session of 1951, then I regret it very much, because I would point out to the minister that the effect of that committee is still felt throughout the country. When you go home you find that -the veterans cannot understand why certain matters in which they were keenly interested were not discussed. The veteran cannot understand why his member was not allowed to bring those matters up before the veterans committee. It is no good trying to explain to a meeting of the Legion the details of parliamentary procedure, terms -of reference and things of that nature.
I suggest to the minister that he adopt the method followed when the late Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie was minister of veterans affairs. I can remember him dealing with a similar resolution and telling us that the -committee would be wide open and that any matter pertaining to the welfare of the veteran would be open for discussion. I notice that there is -a bill on the order paper referring to pensions, and the order paper indicates the three thing-s the bill will cover. I assume that when that bill -comes before

the committee our hands will be tied as far as the Pension Act is concerned except as it relates to those three items.
I would like to hear the minister say right now that the committee will be permitted to discuss any matter referring to the Pension Act. Another matter that I know hon. members will want to discuss is the Veterans Land Act. A case came to my attention only a short time ago where a veteran who had not taken up his reestablishment credit wished to purchase a farm, but he found that that was impossible with the amount of his credit. I think the minister will be the first to admit that farm values have increased greatly, and that veteran found that the $1,200 he was entitled to was totally insufficient. There are many other matters that members of the committee and of this house would desire to have brought before this special committee on veterans affairs.
We probably will not have a committee set up during the session of 1953. I appeal to the minister to say now that any matter pertaining to the welfare of the Canadian veteran can be brought before this committee for discussion.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks are going to be short, sharp and to the point, because I should be upstairs right now at a committee meeting. This matter of setting up a permanent committee on veterans affairs is not new; it has been discussed on several occasions and I am in agreement with the suggestion. In fact I advocated it four years ago.
One of the things I am concerned with is the terms of reference of this committee. Rather than being a committee on veterans affairs, it is being set up as a legislative examining committee. The only prerogative the committee is to have is the right to examine any legislation the government may send to it. There are four bills on the order paper and the committee is to have the right to examine that legislation.
I do not know what the Legion has in mind. The only representations I have seen so far in their publication is with regard to the amendments to the Veterans Land Act. That may be all that they have in mind at the present time. There is one aspect of the Pension Act which I should like to see opened up for discussion. I refer to decisions that disabilities are of pre-enlistment origin. I think there is considerable room for the examination of that type of decision. I know it is based on medical evidence and the attestation papers, but I have seen cases
Committee on Veterans Affairs where the decision was not what it should have been even based on that evidence.
I do not intend to carry on a prolonged discussion. I have always felt that the time to raise arguments of this sort was on the second reading of the bill. I believe the committee should examine the legislation and when it comes back for ratification if we consider there is anything wrong we can argue accordingly.
If the terms of reference of this committee are to be held down, as is indicated, friction and trouble and difficulty will be created. I think the minister would be well advised to accept the amendment moved by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), but should insist that the first order of business of the committee should be to deal with the bills now on the order paper. Then if there are other matters which the committee want to discuss, it would be free to do so.
I am a member of this committee, but I believe that a permanent committee should be set up to examine legislation from year to year. I believe also that the terms of reference of this committee should be broadened so that we may discuss other matters once we have completed the business sent to the committee by the government. That would prevent a lot of friction and difficulty and wrangling in the committee and in the final analysis would save considerable time.

Mr. Speaker, I have advocated the setting up of a standing committee on veterans affairs to deal with problems affecting the veteran. Some years ago when the veterans charter was evolved we thought that that was fine legislation for the veteran, but changes have occurred since that time and there is a great variety of problems that now face our veterans. I am quite satisfied that the terms of reference of this committee as set forth in the resolution are not broad enough. I think that is most unfortunate. When a committee was set up a year ago the Legion presentation of May 17, 1951, had this to say:
Therefore, the Canadian Legion cannot be satisfied with the legislation before this committee. There are no recommendations for improvement in the basic rate of pensions nor is there any mention at all of war veterans allowance, the two principal problems affecting veterans today.
They go on in that vein. I am happy to think that as a result of the efforts of the council of the Canadian Legion and the public as a whole the government were forced to amend the basic pension for veterans during the last session. They did that despite the fact that the terms of reference of the committee of that time did not provide for a discussion of that particular item.

Committee on Veterans Affairs
I think the terms of reference should be made broad enough so that we might be able to discuss all veterans problems. I know that many of the veterans of the present war are finding some difficulty in getting rehabilitated. The Veterans Land Act has been referred to. This act is absolutely inadequate. It was niggardly enough at the time it was brought into being, but with the present increased cost of farm machinery, livestock, land, production and other items it is absolutely impossible for a young man to be set up under that act.
During the past few months a survey was conducted in Ontario to find out what was necessary to set up a young man, not a veteran, on a farm. It was found that it required approximately $15,000. The necessary legislation was introduced into the legislature whereby any young man with the necessary qualifications who has been a resident in the province for three years can be established on a farm with a maximum outlay of $15,000, of which he must supply $3,000.
That is evidence of the total inadequacy of the Veterans Land Act. There is no provision to discuss that act at this particular time and therefore we will not be able to discuss many of the problems facing the veterans of past wars and of the present war. I am sorry the minister has not accepted the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) that any provision of the Veterans Land Act may be discussed by the committee.
Again may I repeat that I should like to see a standing committee on veterans affairs constituted which could consider veterans affairs at each session of the house. I hope the minister will see that the chairman has some latitude, and that we will have broader terms of reference than are provided in the resolution before us so that we can adequately discuss the various problems pertaining to the veterans of this country.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), I am going to make my remarks short and relatively sweet. I must say that personally I am very pleased to see that the government and the minister have decided to introduce this motion providing for the re-establishment of the veterans affairs committee. However, I most wholeheartedly support the pleas of previous speakers as to the necessity for a permanent committee on veterans affairs. Veterans affairs are of such growing magnitude and importance that they require a standing committee to review veterans legislation


constantly and to take note of changing situations and circumstances. A very good illustration was given by the hon.. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) when he mentioned the completely inadequate terms of the Veterans Land Act in some respects so far as settling men on farms under present prices and conditions is concerned. In the second place, the new conditions are creating great difficulties in connection with administration and the giving of satisfactory effect to the terms of the small holdings section of the Veterans Land Act. A great deal of other veterans legislation is constantly affected by changing conditions and circumstances.
I also support the pleas that have been made for wider terms of reference. I think there is no question that the resolution gives the committee wider terms of reference than the motion placed on the order paper at the last session. However, I think the suggestion of members that we should have an opportunity to examine any matter of concern to veterans of this country is sound. I notice the minister is listening most carefully. I hope he has listened most sympathetically to the representations of members on this side of the house with respect to the particular things they have been concerned about this afternoon, the necessity for a standing committee of the house on veterans affairs, and the widening of the terms of reference contained in the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I have been requested by the local command of the Canadian Legion in Essex county, zone 1A, to present their recommendations to this committee. Since I am not a member of the committee I wish to take this opportunity to present their views. Their recommendations are:
1.	That the basic principles upon which war veterans allowance is allowed and paid be unchanged.
Order. Does the house feel that these representations should be presented to the house? Is not the committee being set up so that representations may be made to it?
Surely the debate on this resolution is wide open. I should think the hon. member is in order in bringing forward these suggestions.

The debate on this resolution should not be wide open. Strictly speaking there is no reference in the motion to setting up a standing committee. It has nothing to do with a standing committee. The motion before the house is to set up a select committee. What has been debated has been the

question of whether we should set up a standing committee. No objection was taken, so I did not object. However, if the house feels that the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) should be allowed to present these representations now I will not object.

I want to bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but I am not a member of the committee and probably will not have an opportunity of making a presentation to the committee. Similar representations may be made by other commands of the Canadian Legion. Of that I am not certain, but I have been requested by my local command of the Canadian Legion in Essex county, zone 1A, to present these recommendations. They are as follows:
1.	That the basic principles upon which war veterans allowance is allowed and paid be unchanged.
2.	That war veterans allowance be increased from $40 single and $70 married to $60 single and $120 married.
3.	That the total ceiling be raised to $1,200 single and $2,000 married.
4.	That Canadians who served in England only in the first war be entitled to war veterans allowance.
5.	That widows of imperial or allied services with twenty years' residence in Canada be entitled to war veterans allowance regardless of the date of death of their husband.
6.	That home exemption be raised to $9,000.
I am not making any recommendation personally on behalf of the Legion as to these matters but merely placing them on the record so they will be before the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I merely rise to say that as a member of different veterans affairs committees in the past I have always advocated the establishment of a standing committee on veterans affairs. I am disappointed with the limited terms of reference of the resolution. As we ail know, there are certain weaknesses in various acts dealing with veterans affairs. Some of these weaknesses have been drawn to my attention during the past few months, but under these limited terms of reference I will not be allowed to bring up one of these matters before the veterans affairs committee. For that reason I most strongly urge the minister to enlarge the terms of reference.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution under debate merely mentions one bill, namely, a bill respecting allowances for war veterans and their dependents. I think we all realize by now that there is great need for changes in the
Committee on Veterans Affairs War Veterans Allowance Act. As a matter of fact an attempt was made in the spring session of 1951 to have the question of the War Veterans Allowance Act dealt with, but we were refused an extension of the powers of the committee when the debate took place in the house. Then when the special committee was set up and a motion was moved for a reference back to the house requesting extension of powers so that war veterans allowances could be dealt with by the committee that request was voted down by the government members on the committee.
It was perfectly obvious at that time that there was a need for an increase in the war veterans allowance just as it was obvious that there was a need for an increase in the pension. I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) and his parliamentary assistant have benefited from the trouble into which they hurled themselves last year.
What trouble?

speechtext: Trouble? What do you mean?

They should have brought
in terms of reference containing wider powers for the committee. There is no reason at all why the committee should not be allowed to deal with any matter affecting the war veterans of Canada. It is quite apparent from the minister's reply to the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) that the government will not agree at this time to an extension of the terms of reference, but I should like to have a statement from the minister with respect to whether or not it is the intention of the government to refer to the special committee the other three bills, resolutions for which are on the order paper. For example, order No. 9 on today's order paper is a resolution preceding a bill to amend the Veterans Benefit Act, 1951.
All three will be referred to the committee.

Order No. 10 is a resolution preceding a bill to amend the Veterans Insurance Act, and order No. 17 is a resolution preceding a bill to amend the Pension Act. I am glad to hear from the minister that it is his intention to have all these bills referred to the committee.
In my opening remarks I stated that all the bills would be sent to the committee.
The minister's opening remarks were so short and sweet-
The more reason you should have understood and remembered them.

In fact I do not think he said anything. If he did he was merely mumbling, and I did not hear what he said.

Committee on Veterans Affairs
I do not usually mumble.

I would also ask for a statement from the minister as to whether or not it will be permissible to discuss the problems which have arisen under the Veterans Land Act. If he says those problems can be discussed I have no doubt the committee could put through a request to the house for an extension of its terms of reference in order to deal with them. Someone said here this afternoon it was a great pity that the Department of Veterans Affairs is not now taking the attitude that was taken when Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie was minister, namely, that each special committee on veterans affairs should have power wide enough to enable it to consider any question affecting the veterans at that time; and that this was the proper course for the government to follow. I should hope we would get back to that procedure, rather than limiting the powers of the committee each year.
That brings me to the other point which has been stressed by every member who has spoken from the opposition side of the house; namely, that there should be a standing committee on veterans affairs. Incidentally if there were such a committee it would be able to consider any problem arising in connection with the veterans of Canada, and that is as it should be. We have several standing committees of the house, and I would leave it to the good judgment of hon. members whether any of the committees for which provision is now made have any more importance than a committee on veterans affairs would have. First of all there is a committee on privileges and elections; then a committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines; third, a committee on miscellaneous private bills; fourth, a committee on banking and commerce; fifth, a committee on public accounts; sixth, a committee on agriculture and colonization; seventh, a committee on standing orders; eighth, a committee on marine and fisheries; ninth, a committee on mines, forests and waters. Incidentally, I do not believe that committee has met in the sixteen years I have been a member of this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It meets once a year to
appoint a chairman.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is no recommendation for setting up another committee like it.

A committee on veterans affairs would be different. Then there is the committee on industrial relations, the committee on debates and the committee on external affairs. In addition, of course, there are the joint committees made up of the members of the Senate and the House of Commons. I


believe veterans affairs questions can be compared very reasonably with those having to do with external affairs. There we have a committee which considers the estimates of that department and reports to the house, but there is still opportunity in committee of the whole house for a discussion of each item.
There may have been some excuse for not having a standing committee on veterans affairs when we had only the veterans of the first world war to consider. The problems facing them were largely of a pattern and had been considered for many years in the house, and not many changes could be contemplated. Now, however, we have hundreds of thousands of men and women who served in the second world war, and the problems which have faced and will face them are different from the problems which faced the men and women of the first world war. In addition we have the men who served or are now serving in Korea. Their service will bring up problems different again from those arising out of the second world war.
That can be considered by the committee under that resolution.

I think it would be far wiser and more businesslike to have a standing committee which could follow these problems from year to year. Then we have the men serving in Europe, whose conditions of service are different again, and finally we have thousands of young men and women serving right here in Canada. Our whole defence system has been changed. We have many more people serving in our defence forces than ever before in peacetime and questions are coming up such as whether they should qualify for pensions in the same way as those who have seen active service. Incidentally, I believe the law is too strict now in regard to pensions for those Canadians who have been able to serve only in the defence forces at home. I do not think they are getting adequate consideration.
However, there are all these different conditions which did not exist a few years ago, and the probability is that they will be changing from year to year as time goes by. These problems will certainly be before parliament for many years. It is going to be a long, long time before the last Canadian veteran is off the scene, far longer than anyone in this house will survive. So I do suggest we should give very serious consideration to putting our method of dealing with veterans affairs on a better basis by setting up a standing committee. When the minister closes this debate I hope he will assure the house that this special committee will be permitted to consider whether or not there should be a standing committee on veterans

affairs. That question is one of the most important to be dealt with at this time, and I hope that this special committee will be given the privilege of recommending whether or not a standing committee should be set up.

I would like to join briefly with the others who have spoken, to express the hope that the terms of reference of this committee will not be limited to the comparatively narrow compass which the resolution would seem to indicate. If that is done I think there is no question but that the committee cannot do a proper job. In addition, I am very much afraid that a good deal of the time of the committee will be taken up discussing whether matters which may be brought up come properly within the terms of reference. We have had a great deal of experience with that in some committees in the past. If we are going to be so circumscribed that some of the questions now considered pressing by various veterans organizations across the country cannot be discussed in this committee, then to a large extent the work of the committee will be stultified. I should like to say also that I think the real answer to this problem is a permanent committee such as a number of us have been requesting for a number of years, and I would hope such a committee might be set up.
If the minister speaks now, he will close the debate.

speechtext:
I shall be very brief in closing this debate, Mr. Speaker. Great stress has been laid on the fact that no standing committee on veterans affairs exists. The suggestion has been made that if such a standing committee were set up, it would provide the solution to all problems concerning veterans welfare. To hear some of the hon. members in the house one would think that the mere fact no such standing committee exists prevented hon. members from airing their views or making suggestions concerning veterans affairs. I believe that the debate which has just taken place on this resolution is good evidence to the contrary.
During the course of this debate we have heard hon. members referring to certain problems and expressing their views. All members have the same opportunity on the debate on the address and during the course of the last session I believe they took considerable time, as it was their right to do, to discuss and put forward their views on veterans affairs. Committee on Veterans Affairs course of which members may present their views. Further opportunity is presented when the detailed estimates of the department are discussed, because then every aspect of veterans affairs legislation is open to consideration. When my predecessor was in office the policy was established of setting up the veterans affairs committee whenever the government contemplated important changes in the legislation.
It has been stated that the terms of reference are too narrow, and the committee should be given the same terms of reference as it was given in 1945. The situation in 1945 was completely different from the situation today. During the course of the second world war the government had legislated by order in council concerning the welfare and rehabilitation of veterans of that war. I believe there were some 52 or 53 orders in council which had been passed, and the minister of that day asked the committee to consider all those orders in council and consolidate them into legislation. From that consideration the veterans charter emerged. I submit that the situation today is quite different, and that it is my responsibility- which I am willing to assume and have assumed before-upon the advice of the officers of my department, to introduce the necessary changes to the various parts of the veterans charter. Last year I introduced amendments to the Pension Act, and at that time I undertook to set up this committee. I undertook to introduce during the course of this session amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act, and the resolution setting up this committee is in compliance with my undertaking to this house and to the veterans organizations throughout Canada. Those organizations will come I am sure- they have been invited to come-and state their views to the committee, just as they have in the past.
Furthermore, I want to point out that it is not only when a parliamentary committee is sitting that an opportunity is afforded to organized veterans bodies of this country to present their views to the minister or the Department of Veterans Affairs. Once a year at least, and last year twice, they met with the members of the cabinet, and the door of the office of the Minister of Veterans Affairs is always open to them. I can assure my hon. friends, although it may surprise them, that the members of the executive do exchange views with the minister, and many of the solutions which are found for veterans problems are the result of those exchanges of views. I believe we can proceed with the setting up of this committee to which

Inquiries of the Ministry will be sent not only the legislation conceiving war veterans allowances but various other amendments to legislation mentioned in the resolutions on the order paper. Possibly there will be other legislation; in fact I know of one other bill which is being prepared at the present time.

Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
