I will make the statement first, Mr. Speaker.
Are you playing hard to get?
I have never known the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to be so anxious to hear me speak.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Conscience.

As I mentioned in my previous remarks today, this resolution comes forward as a result of an announcement I made last year, during the course of the last session, at the time when I announced that the Pension Act would be amended. At that time I stated that the government was considering amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act; and that this question was much more complex than that with respect to the Pension Act, where the amendment simply consisted of a percentage increase of the basic rate. It was felt this question would be more conveniently and adequately dealt with by the select committee on veterans affairs and that such a committee would be set up during the course of this session. I also stated that action taken as a result of this procedure would be made retroactive to January 1. That is, any benefits accruing to recipients of war veterans allowance would be made retroactive to January 1.
War Veterans Allowance Act
As hon. members will see, after this resolution has been adopted and the bill is distributed, they will be presented with a completely revised statute, a bill entitled the "War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952" which will replace the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946. In other words, the bill which is to be presented is not merely one containing amendments to certain sections of the act as it now stands, but is a complete revision and consolidation of the War Veterans Allowance Act. It was thought advisable to do this, because, as hon. members know, since it was first enacted in 1930, the War Veterans Allowance Act has been amended on many occasions; in fact, I believe it was amended five times, namely in 1936, 1938, 1946, 1948 and
1950.	It was felt necessary to make some rearrangement of the act so as to present its provisions in a more logical order for the greater convenience of those who have to refer to it.
I wish to point out immediately, Mr. Speaker, that the basic principles of the act have not been changed and that any changes of substance in the bill which will be presented have been made only to render it a more flexible instrument for providing assistance to those veterans and their widows who, in their old age, are unable to maintain themselves or who have no other resources, or whose resources are extremely limited.
May I ask the minister a question?
Yes.
What does he mean by the basic principles of the act?
I mean that there is no change as to the conditions under which veterans can qualify under the act.
You mean that the means test is to be retained?

I mean that the present provisions concerning the conditions under which benefits may be obtained are to be retained. Of course, Mr. Speaker, the most important matter which will be dealt with in the bill is the basic rate of allowances. It is proposed to make a substantial upward revision in these rates. At the same time it is proposed that ceilings for allowable income be also raised in order to bring them more in conformity with the ceilings now existing under the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act. As hon. members are aware, this would allow increases to some pensioners with low disability pensions and others having income other than the war veterans allowance.

War Veterans Allowance Act
A third element is being introduced by this bill. Over the years experience has shown us that a considerable number of war veterans allowance recipients, especially those who are granted entitlement because of having reached the age of 60 without being completely physically disabled, are from time to time able to find some employment of a temporary or a seasonal character, for instance. I think everyone will agree that those who can find such employment should be encouraged to do so. The provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act, as it now stands, sometimes make it impossible to avoid penalizing the veteran who takes employment in that manner. It is proposed now to deal with such veterans whom we may class- and I think those are the words used in the resolution-as marginally employable, and who meet the other conditions of entitlement under the War Veterans Allowance Act by paying them the allowances on a monthly basis when they are actually unemployed and unable to find suitable employment. Without going into the details of this proposal, which hon. members will be able to study when the bill is before them, I might say that the general effect of this proposal would be to exempt their earnings from the operation of the annual income ceiling. There will also be other improvements in the bill, such as the benefits which will be payable to a veteran or his spouse during the twelve months succeeding the death of either of them, and it is also proposed to increase the rates paid to orphans under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Will any consideration be given to Canadians who served only in England during the first war?
I do not think I am expected to give the details of the bill at this stage of the resolution.
You have been giving them, and that is why I asked the question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that this is a measure which all of us in the house welcome; in fact it is one that we have been awaiting for a considerable period of time. The extent to which we will welcome it will of course depend upon the precise terms of the bill, or in other words, upon the extent of the improvements forecast by the resolution and by the remarks which the minister has just made.
In the first place, we are glad to learn ;hat there is to be an increase in the amount of the war veterans allowance. I take it there will be an increase both in the rate paid to single veterans and in the rate paid to married

veterans. I regret that the minister did not see fit to indicate in the resolution that is now before us what the new amounts will be. I had hoped that-
It is improper to do so, I believe, in the resolution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister interjected to say that he believed it is improper to do so.
In the resolution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I suggest the very opposite. Now that this point has come up, Mr. Speaker, I feel I must express my regret that over the past number of years a practice which was followed for decades in this parliament has been allowed to disappear. It disappeared not without my protest on a good many occasions; but the government seems to have been able to get rid of the practice of including in the resolution preceding a bill statements as to the maximum amount of money involved in that bill.
I could take the time, but I will not, to go over bills like the original old age pensions bill, the original family allowances bill, and many others down across the years of the parliament of Canada. In all cases, with very few exceptions, down until 1947, the amount to be provided in the bill was spelled out in the resolution. It was not until 1947 when the old age pension amending bill of that year was before the house that the amount was not included in the resolution preceding any important legislation. Some hon. members will recall the interesting time we had on that occasion. Since then the government has repeatedly brought in resolutions of this kind. I do not think it is fair. However, when resolutions are worded in this way we should be accorded by the rules of the house the right, under citations 439, 445 and 486 of Beauchesne's third edition, to move to increase these amounts when we get into committee on the bill. Whether or not we shall attempt to exercise that right will of course depend upon the provisions of the bill.
This is like a good many other things that happen in parliament, Mr. Speaker. Practices long established are altered on some particular occasion. That change is confirmed by a majority of the house, and in succeeding years we find that we cannot get back to the practice that we thought had been clearly established. At any rate, in addition to the procedural and technical objections that I have now voiced, I express my regret that we have not yet been informed what the amounts are to be.
When I was speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne on March 10 of this year, I urged

that the amount of the war veterans allowances should be not less than $60 a month for a single veteran and not less than $120 a month for a married veteran. Those figures compare with the present inadequate rates of $40.41 for a single veteran and $70.83 for a married veteran. So far as I know, the Canadian Legion has not yet officially changed its request of a year ago for amounts of $50 a month single, and $100 a month married; but I believe that, in view of the increase in the cost of living and the difficulties facing our veterans, the Legion is considering changing that request and asking for higher figures. As a matter of fact, I have before me a letter which I received from Mr. A. Cairns, provincial secretary of the Manitoba and northwestern Ontario command of the Legion, which was dated March 15, 1952. This letter was written to me by Mr. Cairns after I had made the speech in the house which I referred to, the speech of March 10, in which I suggested that the amounts should be not less than $60 a month single, and $120 a month married. Mr. Cairns comments on that in this paragraph:
We feel that the single allowance should be increased to $60 a month and the married allowance to not less than $110 a month which, in our opinion, is the least amount on which the veteran can possibly live in any decency. There is no reason on earth why recipients of the war veterans allowance should be compelled to live in slums. Surely they are entitled to better than that.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the figures which I suggested-and which I suggested on my own-are very close to the figures suggested in that letter by an official of the Canadian Legion in my own city. I earnestly hope that when we get the bill it will have in it figures not less than the figures suggested in Mr. Cairns' letter; I personally still think they should not be less than $60 single and $120 married.
Some hon. members may say: Let us get through this debate and get the bill and find out what is in it. The answer to that, Mr. Speaker, is that the purpose of this debate on the resolution prior to the introduction of a bill is to give hon. members a chance to express their views, and to give the government the benefit of those views, in the hope that the government might look at the bill and see whether it is all that it should be. My hope is that if figures such as I have suggested are not now in the bill, the minister, after listening to the debate that takes place at this stage and in committee on the resolution, will reconsider those figures and raise them, as I say, to not less than the figures suggested in the letter from which I have just quoted from the provincial secretary of the Manitoba and northwestern Ontario command of the Canadian Legion.
War Veterans Allowance Act
As I have said on other occasions, Mr. Speaker, this is a matter in which there is tremendous interest on the part of the Canadian people. That interest is to be found not only among veterans themselves, but among Canadians in all walks of life. People who themselves may have no direct connection with veterans nevertheless feel that Canada should do a lot better for our burnt-out veterans than we are doing at the present time.
I was interested in an exchange that took place a few moments ago while the minister was speaking, when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) interrupted him. We had hoped, many of us in this house at any rate, that when the War Veterans Allowance Act amending bill came before us at this session it would include, if not the complete elimination of the means test, at least very drastic modifications of it. I take it from what the minister has said that although this is a brand new bill which will take the place of the old one, it will be the same in substance in that the war veterans allowance will still be based upon the same principles already in effect.
There are a great many veterans in this country, seventy years of age and over, who are finding it very hard to believe that the means test has really been removed from old age pensions. I have the capacity to explain it in technical terms, but that explanation just does not answer the question in the minds of a great many veterans and a great many widows of veterans. I refer in particular to those who are 70 years of age and over. Since January 1, 1952, they have been drawing old age security pensions. They get the full $40 old age pension because there is no means test on that pension, but they have had their war veterans allowance or their widows' allowance under the War Veterans Allowance Act cut by virtue of the means test that still exists in the War Veterans Allowance Act.
The standard case is the one that has been drawn to my attention by so many persons that I am sure others have had the same experience. It is that of a war veteran who was formerly drawing $40.41 per month but when he started drawing his old age pension of $40 his war veterans allowance was reduced to $10.83 per month, so that his total income would be $50.83 per month, which is within the statutory ceiling of $610 a year.
I should like to hear from any hon. member who has found it possible to explain to a veteran treated that way that he is not under the means test. It cannot be done. You can explain to him for hours on end that the means test does not exist under the Old
1698	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act Age Security Act, but he will come back at you and say that it is there under the War Veterans Allowance Act. He insists that he is under a means test, whereas many other Canadians seventy years of age and over are receiving old age security without having their other income reduced. I contend that this is unfair to our burnt-out veterans.
If the bill does not deal with that problem pretty drastically, if there has not been an examination of the whole relationship between war veterans allowance and the Old Age Security Act, I hope the minister will have that done before he presents the bill to the house. I would remind the minister that the Department of Veterans Affairs has had considerable time to study this matter. As a matter of fact the minister's predecessor and his parliamentary assistant appeared before the special committee on old age security, the sessions of which were held nearly two years ago. It was either in May or in June of 1950 that they attended before that committee so that it was nearly two years ago.
Although nothing definitive came out of the discussions on that point while they were before the committee I think it was made clear to those who appeared on behalf of the Department of Veterans Affairs that the relationship of war veterans allowance to old age security was one that called for exhaustive study and perhaps some brand new basis of treatment. As I say, that was nearly two years ago.
Nearly a year ago-in June, 1951-I urged the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) to have this matter studied during the summer of 1951 so that it could be dealt with in the fall session of that year and so that a new relationship between the war veterans allowance and old age security could be devised and brought into effect prior to the date that the means test would be removed from old age pensions payable to those seventy years of age and over. I was bitterly disappointed last fall when we came here for the fall session to discover, whether or not any study had been given to the problem, that no proposals were forthcoming.
As a matter of fact, hon. members will recall that when we came here last October there was no indication that anything was to be done at the fall session with regard to veterans legislation. In due course, after considerable debate on the floor of this house, we did have the introduction of amendments to the Pension Act with regard to disability pensions, but we were told that war veterans allowance matters would have to wait until the 1952 session. I dared to hope that even with that further delay-as


I suggested it adds up now to nearly two years-we would have an overhaul of the relationship between war veterans allowance and old age security, but from what the minister said today apparently there is to be no change in principle. We are still to have the means test, we are still to have a ceiling on what is called permissible income. Although we have not been given the figures, the minister said that they would be brought more into line with means test provisions of the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act.	.
We shall have to wait until we get the bill to see what those figures are, but I might point out that the ceiling under the Old Age Assistance Act for a single person is $60 per month or $720 per year, and for a married couple, $100 a month or $1,200 a year. I submit that if the new bill provides for ceilings at those levels on the war veterans allowance there is going to be a great deal of disappointment both on the part of veterans who are receiving the allowance and their comrades who are not. There will also be disappointment on the part of Canadians in general that the means test has been continued with the harshness that is apparent with ceilings of that description.
I was glad to hear the statement that veterans over the age of sixty years who can obtain some employment will be treated on a slightly different basis. I take it that their financial position is to be considered on a monthly rather than on an annual basis and that they will get some advantage out of that position. But it is still a means test. The veteran is to be told that in the month he is earning money he will not get his war veterans allowance but that in the month he earns no money and is without other resources he will receive the war veterans allowance.
It has taken a long time in this country to get across to the government at any rate the fact that the people of Canada do not like the means test idea. We have won that point with respect to old age pensions for those seventy years of age and over; we have won it with respect to family allowances. It does seem most unfair that the place where it still remains is with respect to our burnt-out veterans.
I know the kind of problems that arise when you ask for the straight elimination across the board of the means test under the War Veterans Allowance Act along with its elimination under the old age security legislation. I need not go into those problems at this point, but my submission to the government is that it has not tried to find some other relationship that would respect to the extent which they

deserve it the dignity of those whom we refer to as our burnt-out veterans. Surely if there has to be a test of some kind, if there has to be some qualification, if some kind of a line has to be drawn, let us do something that is more dignified, more humane and more Canadian than apply the means test which apparently the government is retaining in the War Veterans Allowance Act.
As I said a moment ago, we welcome the fact that the act is being completely redrawn. I think that is good from the standpoint of administration and of those who have occasion to refer to the act. It has been amended so often that it is difficult to know just what its provisions are without a considerable amount of research. But is not this a golden opportunity to make some of those changes that are so basic?
During the discussions we had, particularly last fall, with respect to the War Veterans Allowance Act the minister did give the assurance that veterans who had been on the allowance, but who lost it on receiving old age security by virtue of the means test in the War Veterans Allowance Act, would not lose any hospitalization or treatment rights which they previously enjoyed. I hope that point will be covered in the bill. I hope that not only will such persons not lose any hospitalization or treatment rights they previously enjoyed but that it will also be made clear that veterans in similar circumstances, who might not be able to qualify for any actual allowance under the War Veterans Allowance Act because of their other income, will nevertheless be entitled to hospitalization and treatment benefits.
Once again, along with others who have made the point by interjections if not in other ways, I want to urge reconsideration of the section of the act which denies the burnt-out pension to veterans of world war I who did not get beyond England. That applies still to a great many veterans, although their number is dwindling, and it applies to quite a number of widows of veterans. These veterans and veterans' widows find it difficult to understand the discrimination against them, particularly when it was no fault of the veteran that he did not get to France in the course of world war I. In world war II England is accepted as a theatre of war but not so in world war I. I feel that change should be made at this session when the act is being rewritten in this way.
It is a good many years now since a former parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs indicated to a group of widows who were here making representations-and I was present when he did so- that he believed that change would be made
War Veterans Allowance Act at the next session. We are still waiting for that change. It would not affect a great many people. Certainly it would not involve many dollars so far as the treasury of the country is concerned, but it would mean a great deal to those affected.
I hope too that consideration will be given, if it has not already been covered in the bill that is to be presented, to the change made a few years ago with respect to imperial veterans who come to this country, and more particularly with respect to their widows. We know that the provision now is that an imperial veteran who has had twenty years residence in Canada qualifies under the War Veterans Allowance Act if he meets the other conditions. His widow, however, does not qualify, no matter how many years she may have lived in Canada

even though she may have been born in this country-if her husband did not himself have the full twenty years residence in Canada before he died. Again the number affected is not great, but it does seem basically unfair that that line should be drawn. I earnestly hope that consideration will be given to this matter.
Members opposite may suggest that one is raising too many details at this time, but I suggest this is the time to do so because of the minister's announcement-it was not clear from the resolution-that we are now getting a brand new War Veterans Allowance Act. That means that each and every one of these points will be before us, and I hope that such debate as may take place now will persuade the minister that if there are weaknesses in the bill in the form in which it is now drafted he should improve upon those weaknesses before it is presented to the house.
A few days ago I directed a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs regarding recoveries where there have been alleged overpayments since January 1, 1952. I had in mind a particular case the details of which I have since sent to the minister. It is the case of a veteran's widow, a lady past 80 years of age, who prior to January 1, 1952, was receiving the widows' allowance under this act, namely, $40.41 a month. That was her total income. She applied, as was her right and duty, for old age security and commenced receiving it in January, 1952. For some reason, which has not been made known to me, the Department of Veterans Affairs did not catch up with this particular case until the month of March. In other words, this lady's war veterans allowance cheque was sent to her in full for the months of January and February. During these two months she got what most of us would like to see all these old people get, both her

War Veterans Allowance Act cheques, the one that she had been getting for years under the War Veterans Allowance Act and the old age security which is now payable to everyone.
In other words, she got a total of $80.41 a month in January and again in February. But when the war veterans allowance board caught up with the case they of course had to point out to her that under the legislation as it now stands she was not entitled to the full $40 old age pension and with it the full amount of the war veterans allowance. It was pointed out to her that her war veterans allowance would have to be reduced to $10.83 a month. In other words, as I said a moment ago with respect to these cases generally, this woman is not under a means test so far as her old age pension is concerned. She gets that $40 in full. But because of the means test in the War Veterans Allowance Act she can have only $10.83 of the so-called burnt-out pension.
In this particular case the war veterans allowance board not only reduced her cheque forthwith, starting with the month of March, to $10.83 so that her total income would be under the statutory ceiling, but they also said to her: Because you have been overpaid in January and February we will have to recover that overpayment. Therefore we are going to take $5 a month off your $10.83 cheque until the amount that you were overpaid in January and February is recovered. So she is now getting only $5.83 where she was formerly getting $40.41. I think it was vicious to do it at all but particularly vicious and unfair in view of the fact that the Minister of Veterans Affairs had announced in the house last fall that any changes made in the War Veterans Allowance Act would be made retroactive to January 1, 1952. If that is done the result in this particular case will be that a little later on this woman's case will have to be reviewed and something will have to be given back to her for January and February of the amount that they are now taking away from her.
I submit that, bad as it was to reduce the amount of the cheque at all, it was adding insult to injury to make a further reduction in lieu of that so-called overpayment. I hope in that particular case-as I say, I sent the details of it to the minister-that the making of that recovery will be discontinued and that the practice will be suspended in all these cases that are brought about in this way until the legislation respecting the War Veterans Allowance Act has been enacted. I think I need say no more at this time. I want to impress upon the minister and the government how strongly Canadians generally feel


about this matter. The burnt-out pensioner is a person whom people in all walks of life feel should get the best possible deal. I hope we will get out of the government a better bill in terms of principles, in terms of the amount of allowance, in terms of the arrangements for other income, than I suspect is coming in view of what the minister has said.
Some time today, perhaps, when we get into committee I hope the minister might also deal with the last clause of the resolution now before us, which reads:
[DOT]-and also to provide for the salaries of members of the war veterans allowance board.
These members are on salary now, of course. I would like to know if the phrase simply means that in the new act provision is to be made for their salaries to be continued, or whether it means there is to be an increase in their salaries. The minister raised a procedural point a few moments ago, and I think he may run into some difficulty if he is suggesting an increase, in view of the fact that the wording of the resolution does not provide for any increase at all. I think at some stage of the game today the minister should tell us what the salaries of the members of the board are now and what changes, if any, are proposed.
In closing, however, I say that the important aspect of the legislation now before us is that we fix the amounts of the war veterans allowance at reasonable levels, that we establish a more dignified relationship between war veterans allowance and old age security than is provided by the means test that is still being applied to the recipients of war veterans allowance, and that we accord the fullest measure of respect and dignity to these deserving fellow citizens to whom we refer so often as our burnt-out veterans, to whom we are so heavily indebted.

My remarks will be brief, Mr. Speaker, because I think we will be in a far better position to discuss this matter after the bill has been brought down. However, I should like to say that we in this group are very glad that a measure to increase the amount of allowance and raise the ceiling has been brought in even at this late stage. I think it would have avoided a great deal of confusion and discontent if this legislation had been brought down in the first session of 1951, before the unemployability supplement had been introduced and before the increase in pensions had been initiated, because, as the

War Veterans Allowance Act
minister knows, there is a great deal of confusion and discontent in connection with this matter, and I believe this legislation will help remove most of it.
This legislation proposes to increase the amount of the allowance and to raise the ceiling; then it provides for assistance to veterans who may be employable in some degree. I was rather puzzled by that, though I suppose it will be easier to understand just what it means when the bill is brought down. Even with the minister's explanation, however, I do not quite understand. I should have thought it would be the other way around, that additional assistance would be provided those veterans who are unemployable. That is what the Legion asked for, because those unemployable veterans cannot take advantage of the casual earnings and make any additional income. This legislation apparently provides for additional assistance to those who can work. It seems to me that is the wrong way around, but as I say it will be better to wait until the bill is brought in.
I also regret that no mention has been made of the declaration of England as a theatre of war in world war I, and apparently no provision is going to be made for the payment of the war veterans allowance to the widows of imperial veterans who have resided in this country for twenty years but whose husbands died before that period of residence had been completed. However, since this is going to be referred to the veterans affairs committee, where I am satisfied it will get a thorough going over, and since I am a member of that committee, I will wait and take up these matters later.

I am going to make the shortest speech in this debate, and ask the minister to remove the means test from the war veterans allowance.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

I would like the minister to explain to the committee what is to be done concerning what is called the war veterans allowance assistance fund. For a few years now a vote has been brought in each year-
It is going to be continued.

-under which a maximum of $10 a month could be paid to a single recipient of war veterans allowance if he had no other income, and a maximum of $15 per month to a married recipient with no other income. In effect payments out of that fund were subject to a second means test, because the veteran had to establish that he had no
other income. I wonder whether that plan is to be continued or whether it has been consolidated with the regular war veterans allowance payments. I notice a vote in this year's estimates for the fund, but I would ask the minister whether it has been consolidated with the regular act.
That fund is being continued, and the same principle will be followed.
The same principle is to be applied?
Yes, in general.

Then I think the committee is entitled to know the conclusion reached by the government as to the relationship of old age security payments to war veterans allowance payments. That question, of course, was brought up on different occasions last year, and now I think we are entitled to know what decision has been reached and what action is to be taken in that regard.

I regret that I do not understand too well what information my hon. friend wants. When the matter came up last session I did explain that we were considering the whole question of the war veterans allowance and its relationship to old age security payments, and that the government would introduce legislation this session as a result of that study. This is the legislation which I am attempting to introduce, and when my hon. friend looks at the bill he will be able to see whether or not it meets with his approval. I do not know just what else the hon. gentleman wants, unless he wishes a long discourse on social security, which I do not think would be proper at this time.
Is the amount of the war veterans allowance to be reduced by any old age security payments a veteran may receive?

This bill changes nothing in any way in regard to old age security payments. It was made very clear last year, by myself when I discussed the matter and when the Old Age Security Act was discussed in the house, that for all purposes old age security payments are considered income. By this legislation nothing is done to change what is in the Old Age Security Act.
Would that not depend on what ceiling is put on?
Yes, within limits.
That will be set out in the bill, of course?
Yes, the amount of the ceiling is mentioned in the bill.

The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend and consolidate the legislation respecting war veterans allowances;

War Veterans Allowance Act
What other legislation, in addition to the present War Veterans Allowance Act, is to be consolidated in the new act?

It is only to include all the amendments which were introduced into the act within the last few years. As I explained in my opening remarks when introducing the resolution, we have rearranged the act and put it in more precise and orderly form for reference purposes. It is more easily understood.
It is really just a revision of the War Veterans Allowance Act itself, and there are no other acts being consolidated?
Including the amendments which are being brought forward.
A few moments ago I asked the minister whether those serving in England would be included in this act. The minister suggested that I might ask that question when we were in committee.
I suggested to the hon. member that he would see the details of the bill when it was distributed.
That is an answer that the minister can give to any question.

It certainly is an answer that the minister can make to any question seeking detailed information. Unless my understanding of the procedure that takes place during the debate on the resolution is wrong, the detailed information is given in the bill. I understand that is the practice which is being followed, and I am sure the hon. member would not like to depart from any established parliamentary practice.

The minister himself has departed from it, and that is why I am asking for the same treatment. The minister might have given the same answer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra or any other member. I should like him to accord me the same courtesy he has shown to them.

I submit the minister is not following out the proper practice. If what he now contends is correct, there is no use at all in having any questions on the resolution preceding a bill. All the minister needs to do is to say "Wait and see the bill." The question asked by the member for Royal is in order, and I submit the minister should answer it. Last year we had the Minister of Justice declining at first to give us the amount of salary that was to be paid, I forget whether it was to judges or some other public servants, but finally it was decided he would have to give the figure. Certainly, we are entitled to have an answer to the question asked by the member for Royal. We are entitled also to know the

ceiling which is proposed, and the amounts by which these allowances are to be increased. All that information is relevant. When the minister answers by saying that we have to wait and see the bill, he makes a farce of this stage in dealing with legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member rising to a point of order?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member did not say that, but merely expressed his views that the minister was not right in his interpretation of the practice in committee. It was for that reason I did not rise immediately to comment on the remarks made by the member for Vancouver-Quadra. It appears to me that members on all sides of the house ask questions of the minister, and the minister who is in charge of the resolution gives replies. It is not for the chairman to direct the type of reply that is to be made. The only rule which I must enforce is that the questions must be relevant to the resolution which is before the committee. I would say that so far the questions which have been asked by the hon. member for Royal and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra appear to have been related to the resolution.
When the minister says certain precise information is contained in the bill, what I believe he has in mind is that he would prefer that the information be given when the bill is being discussed clause by clause; that is his own position. It is not up to me to instruct him as to how he should reply to questions directed to him by any hon. member in the house. I think the hon. member will agree with me.
Your Honour has held that the questions which we asked were relevant to the resolution, and I submit we are entitled to have answers to them.
I believe you stated, Mr. Chairman, that it was not up to you to give instructions as to the type of answer that the minister has to give.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is quite correct.

I have no objection, but I wish to point out that we are now discussing a resolution which reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend and consolidate the legislation respecting war veterans allowances; for increasing allowances and permissible income; for assisting veterans who may be employable to some degree . . .
What is discussed at this stage is whether it is expedient to introduce such legislation, and not the specific details of that legislation. It seems to me it is absolutely improper to go into the details of the bill at the present time.

The question which the hon. member brings up concerns something which would be contained in a clause in the bill. If we are to go through that procedure at this stage, then we would be having repetition when the bill was introduced and was again before the committee.
Mr. Chairman, might I-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Just a moment. I have listened very carefully to the remarks made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs in which he further clarified his understanding of the practice. I am at the moment considering citation 439 which appears in Beauchesne's third edition, which I think perhaps I might read to the committee:
The object of the resolution recommended by the crown is to give the house a first opportunity to discuss the advisability of making certain expenditure. The details of the projected measure are not then disclosed and debate is confined to the resolution which should not be lengthy . . .
I think that both hon. members are quite right in their contentions. According to this citation, the minister is quite right when he says he is not going to divulge the details of the bill at this stage. There is no objection to that. There is no objection, either, to members asking questions about details, so long as those questions are relevant to the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If he gives the details, we shall not need the bill.
If the Minister of Public Works is answering me before I ask a question, that is an innovation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not answering you; I am answering the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.

I believe that on reflection the minister will realize he is establishing something new in the way of procedure, and something which is not in accordance with long established practice so far as this house is concerned. In a case of this kind I have never known such a thing to occur. AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935 (payment for farm storage).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased at this time to move the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, payment for farm storage. The provision permitting the wheat board to pay farm storage was placed in the Canadian Wheat Board Act some years ago. The section of

wheat board shall pay storage if directed by regulation. This bill merely deletes the words "if directed by regulation". If the bill is approved by the house it will make it compulsory on the wheat board to pay for farm storage.
However, I would point out that even with the amendment as proposed by this bill the wheat board would still have the power to set the period during which farm storage would be paid. Even the way this bill is now drafted it would not be mandatory upon the wheat board to pay farm storage for a full twelve months period, but it would establish the principle that the Canadian wheat board shall in each year make provision for the payment of storage for grain held on farms.
In case hon. members representing constituencies outside of western Canada may think that this bill is asking parliament to pay from the national treasury the western wheat farmer farm storage, I would point out that that is not the case. The bill merely provides that part of the farmer's own money which has been obtained by the Canadian wheat board shall be used for the payment of farm storage. This is not an entirely new principle as farm storage was paid during the early years of the war. The mechanics of paying for farm storage are quite simple as the wheat board need merely to increase the initial price paid for wheat by the present storage rate paid to the elevator companies, namely, one-thirtieth of a cent per bushel, per day.
The first point I wish to make therefore is that this bill is not asking the federal treasury to pay the farmer anything; it is merely asking that a certain proportion of the farmer's own money already held by the wheat board shall be paid out in a given way. Over the last few years the difficulties experienced by farmers in marketing their grain in the fall, the fact that there is a growing inventory of wheat being held by the wheat board, indicate that something should be done to ease the situation.
Some farmers find that they do not have the same opportunity as other farmers to deliver wheat to market in the fall. While the country elevator system is spread throughout western Canada, that system along with the annexes and storage space is not distributed in such a way as to give the same market facilities to all farmers no matter at what delivery point they may wish to deliver their grain. The payment of farm storage would assist, in a material way, farmers who are unable to market their grain in the fall.

Certain policies followed in the last few years by the Canadian wheat board have meant that farmers at various points have had little opportunity to market their grain. I do not wish anything I say to be interpreted as criticizing the wheat board, but last fall in particular it adopted the policy of taking short-haul grain to the head of the lakes and to Vancouver terminals first. That meant that in the fall grain was moved first out of Manitoba and Alberta and farmers in certain other areas in Saskatchewan were forced to store grain for longer periods.
The secretary of the Alberta wheat pool points out that it has been the practice in the past for grain to be moved first to the head of the lakes from short-haul points, which meant that Alberta farmers had the greatest difficulty marketing their grain. The payment of farm storage at the rate of one cent per bushel per month would compensate those farmers who have to build additional storage for grain because of the policy adopted by the wheat board or because of non-availability of elevator and storage space.
Another policy followed by the wheat board, and again I am not criticizing it, has resulted in certain farmers having the opportunity to market much of their grain, if not all, much more quickly than others. This was due to the policy adopted by the wheat board of removing quotas for a certain period of time on the higher grades of wheat. Consequently the farmer who had threshed his grain and was fortunate enough to have milling grades of wheat was able to market it in the fall and receive payment for it while other less fortunate farmers had to bear the additional cost of storing grain on their farms.
From my observations with respect to farmers harvesting and delivering grain in the fall I would say that certain farmers, usually the well-to-do ones with modern hauling equipment such as a two or three ton truck, can market larger quantities of their grain, particularly when the quotas are lifted for a period of time, than can the small farmer who must depend on someone else to haul his grain or must use a team of horses or a small farm truck. Farmers who have modern combines and up-to-date machines are also able to harvest their grain earlier than some of their neighbours who are smaller farmers and must depend upon the custom combine or on equipment of their own which is in many cases obsolete.
The payment of farm storage would mean that a farmer who must store his own grain would get a payment of one cent per bushel per month. He would not make a fortune 55701-108J
Canadian Wheat Board Act but he would receive a sum of money which would in part compensate him for the additional trouble of handling that grain three times, once out of the combine, once into the granary and once out of the granary, before it gets to town. I believe it would provide the farmer with additional money to go toward the cost of providing storage on his own farm. It is not a case now of whether or not the wheat board shall pay storage on grain. It is a case of whether we should ask the wheat board to make farmers along with elevator companies eligible to receive the regular storage rate.
I believe the payment of farm storage would also make it possible for a great many farmers to haul grain to the elevator of their own choice. I know that if I belong to the wheat pool organization, as I do, and if I care to, as I have in the past, I can store my grain on the farm even though there is room in a line company elevator and wait until finally there is room in my own wheat pool elevator. In the fall a great many farmers need money right away, and when they find the wheat pool elevator plugged to which they would like to haul their grain they are forced to haul to the line elevator company. If the farmer were paid farm storage he would at least have some small compensation for the trouble of handling his grain two additional times and he would then be in a position to patronize his own co-operative elevator company at a later date.
I believe it might be a good thing-and I ask the minister to give this point consideration-for the government to formulate a policy directed toward keeping on every farm a minimum quantity of grain at least until the middle of the summer. I believe the history of western Canada shows that in one year out of three there is a large area of crop failure. If the farmer in any crop failure area had on his own farm from 500 to 1,000 bushels of wheat he would have in that form some crop insurance and protection against crop failure. I want to point out again that the bill would allow the Canadian wheat board to vary the time over which farm storage could be paid. If there was a crop failure and the wheat board needed all the wheat that farmers could deliver, then of course the farm storage period could be greatly reduced. I doubt very much whether the wheat board is going to have any serious difficulty in the next year or two in obtaining grain to sell. The difficulty that the wheat board may well face is difficulty in being able to dispose of the grain offered for sale.
I believe that if farm storage were paid to farmers it would mean less clamour for available elevator storage space. The little fellow, who is now pushed to the wall in the

Canadian Wheat Board Act fall and cannot get his grain out in competition with neighbours who have modern equipment, would get some compensation, and perhaps at a future date within the crop year elevator storage space would be more readily available. I brought up this subject on December 14, 1951. I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) at that time if he and the government would give consideration to the payment of farm storage. The minister levelled quite a blast at me at that time. I am going to omit quoting that part of the proceedings now, but the minister had this to say-

My hon. friend is practically suggesting that when delivery of grain is made, say in March, instead of getting $1.20, which probably would be due on No. 1 Northern wheat, the farmer would get $1.24. All right, that is 4 cents he is ahead there. But when he gets his final payment he is going to find that 4 cents is deducted. All he gets is 4 cents a little bit earlier. If we changed the interim payment and made it 24 cents instead of 20 cents the result would be practically the same.
I have been attempting to make the point that farmers who must bear the additional cost of storing grain on their own farms should receive compensation. The minister says that all farmers are paid and should continue to be paid the same price for grain irrespective of whether or not they must store it on their own farms. But the minister does not follow that policy with respect to paying storage to elevator companies. He does not say: We will pay all the elevator companies the same storage fee irrespective of the length of time they store the wheat or the quantity they store. On the contrary, storage to elevator companies is paid as it should be in greater amounts to those elevator companies that store larger quantities of wheat for longer periods of time. Just as it would not be fair to pay each elevator company the same storage fee irrespective of the quantity of wheat that the company stores, it is not fair to pay each farmer the same price for a bushel of wheat irrespective of whether or not the farmer must store his wheat for a long period of time. The minister has said that it would not help the farmers at all. I admit that the main result of the bill would be a reallocation or redistribution of farmers' money amongst the farmers. But it does mean that those farmers who must bear the additional cost of storage for a considerable length of time because there is a lack of elevator space or because there is a shortage of box cars or because the wheat board is taking the short hauls first and has removed the delivery quota, would receive some compensation.

Farmers are now paying storage on grain to elevator companies whether they like it or not. The carry-over last July 31 was greater than in the previous year, and there is no doubt the carry-over this year will show a further increase. That being the case, the elevator companies are likely to go on building more and larger annexes. In other words provision is going to be made for the storage of larger and larger quantities of wheat; the farmer is going to pay for that storage, and somebody else is going to get the benefit.
I do not suggest that we should stop paying storage to elevator companies, but I do say storage should be paid to farmers. If that were done I do not imagine the elevator companies would go on increasing the number of annexes so they could store larger quantities of wheat. Last year western farmers, through the wheat board, paid the elevator companies over $17 million. In my opinion the amount paid for elevator storage is likely to increase this year. But I believe it could be held at the present figure of $17 million if farm storage were paid, and any additional storage that might subsequently be needed for grain in western Canada built on the farms so the farmers would receive the benefit.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext: How much was that per bushel?

speechtext:
One cent per bushel per month. The attitude of any western member to this bill should, I believe, depend to a large extent on whether the farmers of western Canada want farm storage. Before I deal with that point I think in fairness I should say that in the correspondence I have had with various farm organizations I have not had strong support for this bill from the farmers' elevator organizations such as the Manitoba wheat pool, the Saskatchewan wheat pool or the Alberta wheat pool; but in the correspondence I have had with these organizations I can say they have not raised objection to this legislation. I think I can fairly interpret their correspondence by saying that for the most part their position was neutral.
On the other hand I have had correspondence with the Manitoba farmers' union who informed me, over the signature of their secretary-treasurer, that they have requested farm storage and are supporting the payment of farm storage; and they point out that they have a membership of over 22,000. Then I come to the Saskatchewan farmers' union, a grass roots farm organization that is strong and active at the present time. Year after year that union has consistently passed resolutions favouring the payment of farm

storage. As a matter of fact just a few weeks ago the Saskatchewan farmers' union presented a brief to the Canadian wheat board, and under the heading of farm storage it had this to say in part:
Another plan to relieve elevator congestion both at local and terminal points and ease pressure on quotas, etc., is a plan of compensation to farmers for grain stored on the farm, especially for grades or kinds of grain not required for immediate marketable positions . . . We would again urge the board to seriously consider implementing a farm storage plan for grain for the new crop year. Such a plan could and no doubt should provide for cancellation of farm storage at any stated date on any given grade or kind of grain required for immediate sale.
Resolution No. 14 at the last annual convention of the Alberta farmers' union reads as follows:
Resolved that this convention go on record as being in favour of the wheat board paying farm storage on undeliverable grain, at the same rate as elevator companies receive.
These statements and resolutions are couched in somewhat different phraseology but I believe those three farm organizations would support wholeheartedly the bill I am presenting to parliament tonight. I might add that at an executive meeting held in Regina on August 29 the Saskatchewan federation of agriculture adopted the following resolution:
That this meeting of the Saskatchewan federation of agriculture request the wheat board to institute a system similar to that in effect in 1941 and 1943 of storage payments on grain stored on the farm.
There we have the farmers' unions of the three prairie provinces, together with the Saskatchewan federation of agriculture, advocating and supporting the payment of farm storage.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, this bill would provide for the reallocation of a small proportion of the farmers' own money. It would provide some compensation to farmers who must store grain on their farms for a longer period of time and consequently must pay an additional cost with respect to storage. The farm organizations I have mentioned support this proposal. In travelling through my constituency and discussing this matter I can say the farmers themselves are almost unanimously in support of it. I believe it only fair that farm storage be paid directly to the farmers themselves, and if that were done we might need even less elevator storage than we now have. So I say the bill I am presenting tonight is in the interests of the farmers and in my opinion is supported by the rank and file western wheat producer.

The hon. member for Assin-iboia (Mr. Argue) has given, Mr. Speaker, a well reasoned argument in favour of farm storage. He said that I blasted him on another occasion. I certainly never intended to blast the hon. member. I consider him a hard working and capable member who is well posted on the wheat situation in western Canada. The section of the wheat board act that the hon. member proposes to amend was enacted in the spring of 1940 and applied to the 1940-41 crop as well as to the 1941-42 crop. The circumstances that caused the amendment of the act were that war had broken out in 1939; transportation to the old country was badly disrupted, markets were disorganized and Canada was receiving very few offers for her crop. At that time it was important to induce farmers to hold grain on their farms to the fullest extent they were able to do so. The clause is, in my opinion, still a valuable clause to be applied in any year that promises to be a year in which wheat does not sell readily. Nevertheless, I cannot agree with the hon. member that it is a clause which should be invoked every year; even when there may be an active market for wheat and when, as this year, wheat can be sold if it can be delivered at seaboard.
I am sure the hon. member will agree with me that no impediment should be put in the way of getting saleable wheat delivered to the wheat board and delivered by the board to ocean ships as rapidly as the market will absorb it. We all know that the successful marketing of wheat and other grains is primarily the marketing of a crop in the year in which it is grown. 1 have been around western Canada for some forty years, and I am well aware that the calamities in the past, involving a sharp fall in the price of wheat, have been caused by

Canadian Wheat Board Act accumulated unsold surpluses from previous crops. It is that situation which I believe should be avoided above all others.
The hon. member has said that no taxpayers' money is involved in his amendments. His proposal is that all the producers of western Canada who market wheat, oats or barley, shall pay to certain producers, who carry their wheat, oats and barley on their farm for a period, storage rates as set out in the bill. I think such payment can only be justified on one of two grounds. The first ground would be: is it to the benefit of all the producers that this should be done? In other words, will all the producers benefit from the money that will be paid to those who collect storage on farm stored grain? The second ground would be that the present system is inequitable, and would there be greater equity as between producers if farm storage were paid?
Now, we will examine the first point: will it benefit all the western farmers if certain wheat or oats or barley is held back on the farms? I see nothing to indicate that that would be the result. As I have said we have today, and have had for several years, a very active demand for Canadian grain. Last year, and again this year, the sales of wheat, oats and barley were limited only by the quantities of those grains that could be delivered in a marketing position at the proper time. Surely, no inducement should be held out to any producer which would induce him to avoid delivering his grain when that grain is needed by the wheat board. The board has to sell wheat well in advance of loading at seaboard, and it can only sell wheat, oats or barley when it is assured that the grain being sold is in a position to permit the carrying out of the contract entered into by the wheat board. With the international wheat agreement, the situation in regard to wheat is not as difficult as it was when wheat was being sold on the open market or to individual customers. The board can have reasonable assurance that the wheat which it sells will be delivered, and it can proceed in its selling with a good deal of confidence, for it knows the selling price of wheat before the season opens, and it also has some reasonable assurance of the quantity of wheat that will be delivered.
Let us take a case that is easier to examine. Let us examine the sale of oats. Now, the active period for selling oats is in the winter months. I have here the prices and sales of oats for the crop year 1950-51, the last full crop year of which we have record. We find that in September, 1950, when deliveries of oats commenced, 7-3 per cent of the crop was delivered and the average price was 88J

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in days gone by I have had a great deal of fun in supporting farm legislation; and when good legislation is introduced at the present time I will be just as energetic as anybody else in the house in advocating it, because I believe the farmers need all the help they can get; and no one is in a better position to give them some help in straightening out some of their injustices than is the minister who has just taken his seat. If he will only ask the Canadian bread eaters to pay the proper price for the farmers' wheat, I for one will be much better satisfied than I am at the present time with our contracts.
With regard to this bill, the main thing it asks for is the striking out-from subsection 2 of section 21, I believe-of the words "if directed by regulation". If the wheat board find it advisable or beneficial to the wheat growers, they have all the power under the present act that is asked for in this bill. Personally, I can see arguments for and against this change. I do not see sufficient advantage in passing this legislation to make the change asked for. I can see that a farmer who is financially able can hold back thousands of bushels of his grain and draw storage on the farm for that grain. On the other hand, I can see a number of the little fellows who have perhaps 500 bushels or 1,000 bushels of grain of their own contributing to pay that storage to the man who is in business in a big way. Therefore while this legislation provides benefits in some ways, it will create injustice in other directions.
Since the act as it stands at the present time contains everything that is asked for in this bill, it is not my intention to support the bill. It has been stated by the mover of this bill that the farm organizations, or the western wheat pools, are neutral. In this instance I believe they are right. I could also be neutral and not vote for or against. I realize that when farm organizations, or any other organizations, meet in convention and have a resolution presented to them-it may be presented by somebody who has not thought the matter all the way through, and he may very easily get that convention to vote for something about which they know very little, or to which they have given very little thought-they may pass it without knowing what they are doing. Perhaps that is what happened with regard to some of the organizations that voted for this out west.


I do not feel that anybody will be injured by our not passing this legislation tonight, because, as I have stated already, everything asked for in this legislation is already contained in the wheat board act as it stands at the present time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR PAYMENT FOR FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this bill also with regard to farm storage. It seems to me that the wrong attitude has been taken with regard to this farm storage. In the first place, the elevator companies take in the grain and get it out to market as fast as they possibly can, in the fall of the year. The farmer does exactly the same thing. He wants to get it to market as fast as he can get it there. The man who is forced to do that is the man who has to sell his grain, the small man, the small farmer who has to sell 500, 600 or 1,000 bushels to pay his debts. He has to sell it at that time.
Let us take the big man, and calculate this on an interest basis. Threshing starts in August. We have August, September, October, November, December, and then January, February and March. Up to February he has six months at 6 cents a bushel for storage. Tell me of any good common-sense farmer who has an amount of grain who would not keep that grain in the granary for 6 cents a bushel for storage? Any rich farmer will keep his right in the granary for 6 cents a bushel for storage. Why should we pass this legislation and allow the rich farmer to receive that gain?
I will agree that the man with 1,000 acres or 2,000 acres down in the southern part of the province of Saskatchewan can afford to do it, but the farmers that I represent certainly cannot afford to do that. They try to get their grain out, and they get it out as fast as they can. Here is another thing that would happen. March and April come along. What would happen is what happens in the fall. Manitoba floods out everything. If we were to have the farm storage proposition we would have that happen in April because all these men down there would naturally keep their grain if they could get that large amount for storage.
Take the situation as it stands today. The minister has told us that he can sell this grain as fast as he can get it. The man in the country who is going to get 6 cents a bushel for storage on his grain is naturally, beyond any shadow of a doubt, going to keep that grain. Why would he keep it? He would keep it because there are two things that he will get out of it. In the first place he is going to be sure that he has a crop. If he does not, he keeps that grain. In the second place, he is going to be well paid for it, and

we, the smaller farmers, are going to have to sell our grain in the fall of the year, or during the winter months, and then we are going to have to pay the rich farmer, too. It is all going to have to come out of that amount.
If you are going to sell an article you have to put it in the place where you can sell it. We have not got enough transportation in western Canada to draw even 40 per cent of the crop in the last two months of the year. I am sure that if we had the transportation to do the work, which we have not, in the final analysis, we would bog down because of the large surpluses that would be built up, owing to the amount that was being paid for that storage. The farmers would not think about storage; they would think of the dollars that they were going to get out of it. I am sure that the majority of farmers in the eastern part of the province of Saskatchewan certainly do not want farm storage.
