subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when this debate was adjourned last Friday evening I was about to deal with family allowances and old age security. Since that time we have had a debate on the Family Allowances Act, during which much useful information was disclosed. However, the fact remains that the payments made under that act today are not what they were when it was enacted in 1944. They do not have the same purchasing power; instead of being the payments they were, they are considerably reduced. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) discussed this subject very thoroughly, and I admired his courage and the way he put forth his views. He praised the Liberal party for bringing in family allowances, and said it was the first party in this country to think of them. I suggest that the Social Credit party in Alberta was the first party to suggest that dividends be paid to the people of this country, and without a means test.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But you never paid them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is true that the Liberal government has come a long way toward meeting our requirements. It is also true that we do not agree with the way they collect the money with which to pay these allowances. The fact is that the Social Credit party of Alberta was the first party in Canada to suggest a dividend.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They suggested it, but they never paid it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will handle you in a minute. I agree that any time we add to the purchasing power of the common people we are doing something good. If in 1930 or even 1937 or 1938 we had suggested that $322,150,000 be distributed, you know what would

The Budget-Mr. Wylie have happened. They would have said that was inflation; that we would be giving the people something for nothing, and we would ruin everyone. If that money had been distributed in those bad years-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where were you going to get it in those years?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The same place we would get it today. If that had been done we would not have had the suffering we saw in many parts of this country. Perhaps the hon. member who is interrupting me did not go through that. I doubt if he did. He looks very well fed, and I imagine he was well fed in the thirties, from the way he talks. When we did suggest the distribution of a dividend in 1933 and 1934 and up to 1937, they said it could not be done, that we would have inflation. Well, I would sooner have inflation any time than deflation. When we have inflation, within limits, people have money; but in those tough years when we had deflation no one had any money. The trouble was that we produced so much everyone had to starve. I remember that I was employed by the Alberta government as an agricultural field man on relief work. The dominion government shipped in carloads of cheese, beans, creosoted fish and everything else to be distributed by the mounted police among the recipients of relief. At the same time people running stores in those towns and villages were going broke because they had too much of those goods on hand and could not sell them. Is that the way you want to live? I don't. I saw what happened, and we do not want that to happen again.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It won't, under a Liberal government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Under a Liberal government? Surely you do not want me to start in on the Liberal government. If you do I can do it, and I can tell you plenty. Talk about the poor prices being paid for cattle today. Think what the Liberal government did back in 1937 and 1938, when they bought our cattle for a cent a pound. Don't ask me about the record of the Liberal government in the purchase of cattle. I had no intention of getting into this, Mr. Speaker, but the hon. member asked for it and I gave it to him.
In connection with old age security, together with the other members of this group I was very happy to see the means test removed at the age of 70. One thing we did disagree with was the amount paid. Today Liberal members get up and praise the Liberal government for removing the means test. That was done by unanimous consent of the house. Having had eight years of


experience in handling old age pensions over a very large area, I knew what conditions were, and I was glad to see the means test abolished. It enabled some people to receive the benefits who otherwise would have been disqualified. But the dominion government has done one thing by paying only $40 per month. It has forced every provincial government to use a means test in connection with any supplementary pensions. I know that is the case in Alberta, where we pay one of the highest pensions in Canada to our aged citizens. We pay $10 a month plus all medical and health benefits, but that comes under the means test. We render the same assistance to the people from 65 to 69. Not only that, but in Alberta we pay a pension of $40 per month to widows who are between 60 and 65. What other province pays a pension to widows? Certainly the federal government does not but the government of Alberta does.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How many widows?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sure that if you lived in Alberta there would be another widow.
Mr. Speaker, those are the facts, and that is what Alberta is doing; but we are forced to do it under a means test. I am sure that Saskatchewan and British Columbia use the means test on their supplementary payments. Perhaps Ontario does, too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ontario does not have a supplementary payment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Hellyer) says that they do not have a supplementary payment in Ontario. In other words, the old age pensioner must get along on the $40 per month. I am sure there are plenty of Conservatives from Ontario here who could correct that statement if it were wrong. In Alberta, we do have a supplementary payment, because that province is one of the top provinces so far as provision for old age security is concerned.
The other evening I listened to a very interesting speech delivered by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver). It was a very enlightening speech. He showed us what could be done in that northern part of Manitoba, and what can be done in northern Manitoba can be done in Saskatchewan and Alberta. Those areas hold untold wealth. We know there are many thousands of acres of agricultural land and thousands of acres of minerals that have not yet been explored. While I listened to the hon. member I could not help but think about the southern and central part of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and the development that we could have in

those areas. I am going to speak about Alberta, because I know more about that province than any other.
In Alberta we have three large irrigation schemes that are being developed. There is the St. Mary's-Milk river, the Bow river project and the Red Deer river diversion. If those three projects were fully developed, and we hope they will be in the very near future, they would bring into the irrigation area close to 900,000 acres with a potential for the establishment of perhaps 10,000 or 11,000 farms. This area is well served by railroads, highways and other services which must be taken into consideration in developing communities. In the southeastern part of Alberta we consider every year a dry year. Last year was an exception, and we had an abundance of rain. As a matter of fact, we had so much rain we could not get our crops harvested, which is very unusual for that area. However, over the years the people of the drought area expect every year to be a dry year. This year the area is starting with an abundance of subsoil moisture. As a matter of fact, there is from four to five feet of subsoil moisture which is more than we have had for thirty years. It does not mean that we are going to have a crop. The southern portion of the province is subject to these Chinook winds which will dry up a crop in about five days. As a matter of fact I have seen a crop standing four feet high, and within one week it has been wilted to such an extent that you could see the rows in which it was seeded right across the field. It is for that reason we need these three irrigation projects, and that is why we must continue to work in spite of the floods we had this year.
I might say that Medicine Hat experienced this year one of the worst floods it has had since 1918. A thousand people had to leave their homes. I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is not here, but it does seem to me that the P.F.R.A. should use its power to establish dams in that area so that the water could be stored. One of the main causes of the flood at Medicine Hat was the dam on Seven Persons creek. While the dam did not go out the spillway did, and the results are the same.
What happened with regard to the Ross creek project? P.F.R.A. administration had all the supplies in there in order to put in head gates on the canal and to divert the creek into the canal, but they were moved away before the diversion was completed two years ago. The result was that a year ago this spring the main highway leading south to an important farming district was flooded to a depth of several
The Budget-Mr. Wylie feet of water. The farmer's yard where the diversion is located was washed out to a width of about 20 feet, with water to a depth of 14 feet. This year the P.F.R.A. administration had to repair that damage. It has cost them thousands and thousands of dollars to do what they should have done in the first place, namely, to put in proper head gates in the canal. At the present time the head gates are not in the canal. This means that our reservoir is not full because we could not turn the water in.
In this house we talk about saving money in the estimates. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) mentioned many ways in which this could be done. I mention this one tonight. When we have the goods on the job, let us use them and finish it. But they were moved away. I would not venture to say that .they were playing politics by moving them away but I believe that is exactly what happened.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did you ask them?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did. That is what happened. The job was not completed. The storage of water in southeastern Alberta is extremely important to that area.
Another matter that must be looked into is another storage dam on the Bow river. That is of great importance. The farmers of the eastern irrigation district are worried lest they will not have enough water when a dry year comes along. They have a right to be worried, because when we put another 400,000 acres under water on the Bow river development project it is certainly going to require all the water that we can store. There is only one solution, namely, to build another dam on the Bow river. The more we do in that line, the more we are going to save for the people of Canada.
We want more people out west. Certainly we do. There is only one way in which we are going to get them and that is by developing our natural resources. Alberta is today doing a good job in developing her natural resources. I do not have to tell hon. members that, because they all know it. But we must have more development in the way of irrigation and we must have more people to settle on the land. In that way they will be producing something that will be of benefit to Canada.
We as members of parliament must have not only a provincial but a national outlook. Too many Canadians today do not believe that anything which benefits one part of Canada benefits the remainder, but it does. Let us work together so that we can develop this country from one end to the other.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should

The Budget-Mr. J. A. Ross first of all like to refer to a statement made by my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). As reported of page 1474 of Hansard he stated:
. . . there is not much satisfaction to many of our taxpayers to hear these millions and billions bandied about-they do not live in a world of millions and billions; they live in a world of fives and tens, and less than that. It is the ordinary taxpayer that I am interested in, and it is the ordinary taxpayer that this house exists to protect.
I think there is a great deal of food for thought in that statement made by the hon. member for Greenwood. I believe that important fact is all too often overlooked in this chamber.
This has been a huge budget, one of approximately $4-5 billion, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) left with us to discuss and to debate in this chamber while he departed to the south for some days. We have been rather accustomed to the phraseology of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to the effect that we might save a million dollars, but what is a million nowadays? I am afraid that has become rather the mental attitude of the government of the day in taxing the people and in the expenditure of our money.
A great deal of this budget is for national defence. Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to an editorial in the Globe and Mail of April 26. It is headed "$18,000 Per Man" and reads as follows:
If money is the sinews of war, Canada's armed forces should be the most formidable the world has ever seen. They are certainly the most expensive the world has even seen. Never before in history has a nation's armed forces cost it more than $18,000 per man. Even today, no nation comes close to that figure-including the United States, which is supposed to be the most extravagant in its military spending.
It is a matter of simple mathematics. Canada's defence budget, exclusive of foreign aid, is $1-7 billion. Our armed forces number 94,000. This is just over $18,000 per man. The U.S. defence budget, exclusive of foreign aid, is $51 billion. Its armed forces number 3-5 million. This is just under $15,000 per man.
How about Britain? During the present fiscal year, that country will spend $3-9 billion on defence. She has 850,000 men under arms. Thus, her cost per man is just over $4,500. Australia's defence budget this year is $300 million. With forces of 50,000, her cost per man comes to $6,000. Belgium's forces total 140,000, with a defence budget of $460 million; slightly over $3,000 per man.
It is true, of course, that the emphasis in Canada's defence program is on the air force-most expensive of all services. Our cost there runs around $25,000 per man. But Britain seems to manage it on slightly under $5,000 per man. As for the army, Britain gets 440,000 men for her $1-4 billion-slightly less than $3,500 per man. Canada gets 48,000 men for her $532 million-slightly more than $11,000 per man.
It is also true that Canada labours under the handicap of her relatively small population; and hence her relatively small armed services. A nation numbering its troops in the thousands will natur-
IMr. Ross (Souris).]
ally have a higher per-man cost than one which numbers them in the millions; which has the advantage, so to speak, of mass production.
But the fact remains that our per-man cost is markedly higher than the American; three times as high as the Australian; four times as high as the British; nearly six times as high as the Belgian.
This newspaper does not argue that a per-man cost of $18,000 is unjustified. It can be justified- but only in one way. We are only justified in having the most expensive troops in the world if they are best-trained, the best-equipped in the world. We are only justified in paying the top price if we get the top return from it. Are we, in fact, getting the top return? Are we getting our $18,000 worth?
The fact is that we are not. We have none of the tanks which make the British divisions the hardest hitting force in western Europe today. The best we could put into western Europe, or into Korea, was infantry-well-trained, and efficient, but not expensive. The story of our air force does not need repeating. Whatever may be the deficiencies of the British, the Americans, even the Belgians, they are ahead of us. These being the facts, what has been done with our money?
That is very indicative of the thoughts of many of the taxpayers of Canada today.
It has been pointed out also by the hon. member for Greenwood in his discussion of the defence department that there was an item of some $4,890,000 for telephones, telegrams and communication services in a year. That seems out of all proportion. There are huge sums spent on government travelling and removal expenses, and many millions are spent on the publication of departmental reports and general publicity in that way.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) spoke to the house, and is reported at page 1530 of Hansard as having said:
Where, in the world today, is there any country whatsoever with a sounder economic position, a better fiscal policy, better development, or a higher level of employment than this country of Canada under the present Liberal administration?
He implied that everybody should be very happy in this country. Well, Mr. Speaker, I, like many other people, for many months past, have been very worried and concerned about the general plight of agriculture from coast to coast in this country of ours. I can tell you that many of these farm people are greatly worried, and in my opinion have reason to be so worried. In many cases the beef producers are without a market, and with the announced floor of from 7 cents to 10 cents a pound below the market of some few months previous many people are now out the value of feed and labour during the winter months, along with a further loss of cattle values.
This has been a very serious business in respect to them. They have been greatly aggravated by the disastrous outbreak of foot-and-month disease. I am sorry to hear of the recently announced outbreak in various

other areas. It is certainly playing havoc with the beef industry of this country and with our general economic situation.
The Winnipeg Tribune of April 23 carried the following:
City packing house executives state that they cannot take the financial risk of paying floor prices for cattle, when Ottawa gives them no guarantee against loss.
This was written some days following the announcement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that these floor prices were now in operation throughout this country. I can tell you that there were several very unsatisfactory days in the St. Boniface stockyards adjoining Winnipeg.
There was a floor price of $22.80 per hundredweight announced for good steers, and a floor price of $24.50 for grade A hogs. But the price being paid in Winnipeg yards for heavy hogs and sows has been approximately 14 cents. That is a very great difference, and it is creating great hardship for those producers in the matter of marketing their hogs.
The cattle market has been at a stalemate for several days, with no sale whatever for certain grades of cattle. We had the plight of the poultry producer, and an unsatisfactory price for eggs. The plight of the dairy producer, and especially that of the cheese producer, with no market for their products, has been referred to. If there is a floor provided for hogs, for poultry and for other products, the cheese producers of this country are every bit as much entitled to a floor price during these very difficult times.
It has been pointed out in this debate that Canada's farm population of some 450,000 are dependent on receipts from the dairy industry as a source of income. It contributes more than $600 million to our national commerce. As was pointed1 out by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), a large area of Canada is peculiarly suited to this form of farming, and it requires years of labour to build up a good dairy herd. The present situation in the dairy industry constitutes a national emergency. The outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease that I have referred to has resulted in the loss of the United States of America market for dairy cattle, as well as for beef. The traditional United Kingdom market for cheese is lost, and there is a quota imposed by the United States of America against Canadian cheese.
The government have announced the policy of support prices for certain agricultural products which, as I stated, is also applied to the cheese producers. The apple producers of this country are facing loss of markets. Then we have the western wheat producer who
The Budget-Mr. J. A. Ross has subsidized the consumers of Canada and of the United Kingdom by several hundreds of millions of dollars during past years, and they are still continuing to do so.
There is the matter of the international wheat agreement and the policies of this government which have been responsible for this. While we have been urging the government for some years that the domestic price of wheat should be different from that prevailing under the international wheat agreement, nothing has been done. Again I want to appeal to the responsible minister and to the government that there should be a different price for the domestic wheat of this country.
On April 16 at North Portal, North Dakota, the American farmer was receiving $2.09 a bushel for his wheat, while across the street at North Portal, Saskatchewan, the Canadian farmer received $1.43J per bushel for a like grade of wheat. In the United States of America the federal treasury subsidizes the farmer for the prevailing difference in the market price and the price under the international wheat agreement. According to the Searle Grain Company research department, this will cost the United States of America taxpayers around $600 million during the term of this international wheat agreement. While we have lost many of our best agricultural products, the price of our products is rapidly decreasing, the cost of production is still increasing. The cost of farm machinery increased during the year 1951 by over 14 per cent, and further increases are expected. Farm wages are at an all-time high, and still rising.
The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Catherwood) pointed out the fact that we at one time enjoyed a splendid market for many of our agricultural products in Britain. In 1938 we supplied 27-5 per cent of the total British imports of barley. This market is now entirely lost to Russia. In 1938 we supplied 93 [DOT] 9 per cent of the total British imports of oats, and this market is lost. In 1945 we supplied 43 per cent of the total British imports of beef. This market is lost to the Argentine. In 1945 we supplied 83 per cent of the total British imports of bacon. This market is lost to a very great degree. In 1945 we supplied 31 per cent of the total British imports of cheese. There has been a great loss of this market. In 1947 we supplied 18 per cent of the total British imports of poultry. We have lost this market chiefly to iron curtain countries such as Poland and Hungary. In 1948 we supplied 79 per cent of the total British imports of eggs. That market is completely lost.

The Budget-Mr. J. A. Ross
These figures indicate, Mr. Speaker, that we are facing the most serious financial and trade crises in our history, and it is a dark picture for Canadian agriculturists during these times. With Canada being the only dollar member of the commonwealth our markets have been practically erased. This party has asked the government to initiate a trade and economic conference of members of the commonwealth, but up to the present that request has been refused. It is most important that to some degree Canada should regain its traditional markets for primary products. Our loss of markets has brought about a situation that strikes at the very roots of the agricultural economy of Canada.
As already set forth by the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), Canada is short of tanks and planes. The British Centurion tank is considered one of the best of its type in the world and it sells for much less than other types. The British Canberra bomber is so good that the United States are making it for themselves. Our armed forces are very ill-equipped and if Canada for the time being were to buy Centurions and Can-berras in some quantity the British would have dollars with which to buy Canadian agricultural products.
I urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who is also the Minister of Defence Production, to do something about this. I think the minister should be able to work out some scheme which would be beneficial both to the armed forces of this nation and the agricultural producers of Canada. I trust the government will endeavour to take some action such as this.
Before closing I should like to make some reference to this dreaded foot-and-mouth disease. I was surprised at what took place in this chamber yesterday with respect to a motion that had been passed previously by the house. I know the matter is to be discussed by the standing committee on agriculture, but that committee has not yet been convened. While I am anxious to get to the bottom of the cause of the great delay in taking action once the disease was first discovered I want to make it clear that I do not want to be responsible for keeping these veterinary officials away from that area in Saskatchewan while the matter has not yet been cleared up. The committee is to be convened tomorrow to investigate this serious matter. I think this is one of the most serious things that have struck this nation in its entire history. We cannot begin to predict its effect upon our economy. While it has been decided to place the matter before the agriculture committee I think we 
should be most careful to see that the services of these officials are used to the best advantage in trying to stamp out this disease.
When the minister made his announcement that the disease was under control I sincerely hoped that he was right, but I along with others said that we must keep our fingers crossed until the first few weeks of spring had passed. The new outbreak has occurred during the last few days and I sincerely hope that this will be checked as soon as possible.
I should like to have the minister point out in more detail how the floor price on beef is to operate. I have before me the last copy of the Manitoba Co-Operator which contains an article headed "Who Benefits?" and which reads:
In the March 27 issue of the Manitoba Co-operator an editorial appeared, entitled "Ten Provinces- Eleven Problems." A suggestion was made that it was imperative in the interests of the livestock industry of Canada to remove all provincial embargoes and turn the problem of dealing with the foot-and-mouth disease entirely over to the federal government, whose sole responsibility it was in the first place.
Livestock markets in western Canada are still chaotic and will no doubt remain so until all interprovincial embargoes are removed. With the United States market closed and with our present level of livestock production in Canada, it is unlikely that the domestic market will absorb all that is offered for sale in the next few months, unless the retail price drops to a corresponding level of that for live cattle.
It is interesting to note that one large retail outlet in the city of Winnipeg quoted blade rib roast of beef at 63 cents per pound on February 25, the day that the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease was announced. On April 17, the same cut of beef was advertised at 62 cents per pound. In spite of this, cattle have dropped nearly five cents per pound in that time. The question farmers would like answered is, why have not retail prices been reduced more than one cent per pound?
The recent announcement from Ottawa that a support price for cattle has been established at 25 cents per pound basis Toronto for good steers (dressing 53 per cent defatted or 55] per cent fat in), has been met with criticism from farmers. In order to determine the dressing percentage cattle must go to packing plants for slaughter prior to establishing the price. This means that carcass grading for cattle has been foisted on the unsuspecting farmers much as carcass grading for hogs caught them unawares a number of years ago.
The support price applies to four classes of cattle -choice, good and medium steers and heifers, and choice cows. At the time of going to press, no announcement has been made as to the price differentials at the St. Boniface market.
As far as can be determined, the support price does not necessarily mean that cattle will be bought at that price. In our opinion, it actually means that the federal government guarantees to buy any surplus stocks of beef from packing plants at the equivalent of that price. At present prices for cattle at St. Boniface are three cents below the support price.
In view of the fact that the producer is being blamed for the high cost of living, what the farmer would like to know is who is getting the difference? The consumer is paying nearly the same price for

beef, while the farmer is getting five cents per pound less than he was two months ago, and has little or no guarantee that the price may not go lower.
Can it be that the meat trade has outwitted the government officials, by absorbing the differentials?
This is a most serious situation and I hope the Minister of Agriculture will give more details to the house and to the producers of this country of the operation of the floor price on beef. There has been great dissatisfaction with respect to this as well as with respect to the floor price on hogs. In many instances the prices are not going through to the producers of cattle and hogs. I trust that steps will be taken to clear up the situation as soon as possible.
I make a final appeal to the government to try to work out a scheme to try to hold stable markets for our agricultural products. I have suggested a scheme whereby most useful equipment for our armed forces could be exchanged for primary products.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Murphy five months! This is despite the fact that they wrote millions of dollars' worth of insurance in every city, town and hamlet throughout northern Ontario.
This brings me to another aspect of the situation, namely, that all these millions are being drained out of northern Ontario and invested in certain selected areas of southern Ontario. Our own money is being used to build up better housing'in southern areas to compete further with our northern Ontario centres. I am also informed that these companies are pursuing a policy of lending only to select risks in certain areas of these southern centres. In other words, they are just skimming off the cream.
It has been further suggested to me that these companies are permitted to use their own discretion as to where housing is needed and as a result are lending only in certain areas. I should like the minister to clear up this point. Surely such a policy cannot be condoned by the government when we need a program that will build homes in every community across the nation. I would urge the government to call a conference immediately with these lending institutions through the appropriate channels, get this phase of building under the National Housing Act under way again, and insist that the companies earmark a reasonable portion of their available funds for this purpose.
I would further urge that if this cooperation is not forthcoming the government should then change its policy and should expand the facilities under section 31A which permits direct loans. I admit that I do not favour the federal government becoming a large-scale landlord, but I feel the present situation demands immediate attention. I believe, if the government points out to the lending institutions their responsibility at this time, together with the suggestion that the government is prepared, if necessary, to enter this field itself, that then and only then will our housing program be resumed, and then and only then can the minister say, as he has said on previous occasions, that the lending institutions are playing their traditional role in this field. By such action as I have suggested we can make sure that all our people have the opportunity, if they so desire, to build under this plan.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland), and I have no hesitation in saying that what he said was certainly factual and, unfortunately, only too true. I agree entirely with the earlier part of his speech. I think

the only part I disagreed with was when he said so much of the money these insurance companies were draining out of northern Ontario was coming into southern Ontario. I can tell him that we have the same complaint in western Ontario as the hon. member so ably described in the few short minutes he took up tonight discussing this very important subject.
I have for a number of years concerned myself with the question of federal taxation and its relationship to crown corporations and municipalities in this country. I am glad that the government has gone part way, at least, in recognizing the seriousness of this situation growing up within our economy, and that today we have the Abbott or government formula as laid down for crown companies, which is quite satisfactory. I am also glad that the government has taken the step it has in the way of grants in aid to municipalities, where federal property constitutes 4 per cent or more of total assessments. Beneficial and all, however, as this change may be, no one, I am sure, agrees that the problem has been satisfactorily met.
Twelve years ago in this country the federal government took 49 cents of every tax dollar, leaving 51 cents to the provinces and the municipalities. Today, the federal government absorbs 73 cents out of every tax dollar, and the remaining 27 cents leaves the municipalities and the provinces to get along as best they can. While this whole question of federal, provincial and municipal taxation warrants considerably greater study than has yet been afforded this problem in view of its gravity, the immediate question is what can and should be done to assist financially pressed municipalities, and we find those from coast to coast.
The present tempo of development and industrial expansion in this country has created for many municipalities problems with which they are unable to cope. Increased demands for educational costs, services for housing and numerous other requirements are today bringing the burden of municipal taxation to the point where that long-cherished hope of owning your own home is being questioned.
The present policy of the government of grants in aid to municipalities is reserved to those areas where federal property exceeds 4 per cent of the total assessment. In my opinion, all federal property should be subject to regular municipal taxation, and I urge the government to give consideration to this problem at the earliest opportunity.
I listened with interest to the Minister of Finance when he presented his budget in this

house on April 8 last, and I was impressed with the marked similarity between this budget and the one presented in the preelection year 1948. I have since re-read the minister's budget presentation of 1948 and also his presentation in the pre-election budget of 1949. In the pre-election budget of 1949, when the minister announced sweeping tax reductions right across the board, he had this to say at page 1795 of Hansard:
... I feel the time has now arrived when this parliament should enact some further substantial reductions in taxes. The increasing flow of goods available for sale to consumers without higher prices makes tax reductions economically feasible. The prospective surplus of revenue over expenditures, in the absence of tax changes, and even of a substantial cash surplus over our requirements for income and investments make tax reductions financially feasible. The reduction of more than $1,600 million in our net debt made in the last three years has put us in a position now where we may prudently give consideration to further tax reductions. Finally, sir, I should say, that I have been led to believe in recent months, as no doubt other hon. members have, that most of the Canadian people would support and even welcome an enlarged measure of tax reductions this year.
Those were the minister's words. Compare the situation then with the situation now. Economically feasible then, because of the increasing flow of goods available to consumers, but not economically feasible today when goods are not only available but in many industries are piled up in inventories, causing widespread unemployment. Financially feasible then, because revenues exceed expenditures. That situation is just as true today when we have before this house estimated expenditures which the minister himself admits exceed what the government expects to spend.
In this regard, I do not think the Minister of Finance, any more than the Minister of National Defence, can do more than say "We think this vote adequate for what we may require." The record of the past few years has conclusively proven that defence expenditures have been overestimated. This, combined with continuing high revenues exceeding estimates, has resulted in surpluses far exceeding estimates given to this house. Reductions prudent then, because since the war we had reduced the public debt by $1,600 million. Surely this reason is just as valid today, when we have reduced the public debt by $2,344 million, as it was in 1949.
The fourth reason given by the minister at that time was that the Canadian people would support and even welcome an enlarged measure of tax reduction. On April 8, when the budget was presented to this house at page 1260 of Hansard, Minister of Finance told us that-
Unless conditions at home exceed my generous expectations, and unless the clouds that overhang
The Budget-Mr. Murphy the international scene lift more rapidly than we now have a right to expect, my hope for next year is the same as that expressed a year ago, an expectation of no increase in tax rates, but not much likelihood of substantially lower rates.
A week later however, speaking to the voters of this country in a "Nation's Business" broadcast over the C.B.C. national network, the minister had an entirely different story, when he said-
I hope that before too long the international situation will make it possible to make some bigger tax reductions than we have been able to make this year.
Just what happened in the international scene during that week that warranted this change of assurance to the Canadian voter has never yet been explained by the Minister of Finance. This similarity of factors and apparent predication of reasoning to suit the circumstances leads me to believe that if there ever was a time when estimates should be gone over with a fine toothed comb, it is this year. I hope the government will see fit to afford parliament the opportunity to do this, instead of the usual practice of voting millions a minute in the dying days of parliament.
I want to discuss another matter, Mr. Speaker, the gravity of which is increasing year by year, and which constitutes a problem which I think warrants top-level consideration by the federal governments of this country and the United States. I refer specifically to the increasing damage as a result of high water levels in the great lakes system, and the inadequate action taken by responsible governments to meet this situation. Personally I am in favour of the St. Lawrence waterway development, but I am not carried away with the idea that this will be accomplished at an early date, or even undertaken within the next year or so. In the meantime, and as part of any St. Lawrence waterway development consideration must be given to the disastrous effect of rising water levels in the great lakes system.
I do not intend on this occasion to reiterate the extensive damage that already has been caused, other than to point out that in my own constituency valuable lake shore property has been damaged severely and it has been necessary to move and rebuild a lake shore road on three different occasions within the last twenty odd years, always in the expectation that this action would be adequate, only to find that the problem was becoming worse. Press reports would indicate damage in the millions in various other parts of the province of Ontario, and I think this government is well aware of the serious damage already done.
1724	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Murphy
The suggestions I propose to make to this house today have been considered in line with the possibility of the eventual St. Lawrence waterway development and would, in my opinion, fit into such a scheme.
The great lakes, having a surface area of over 95,000 square miles and a drainage basin of approximately 298,000 square miles, are the headwaters of the St. Lawrence river system. In comparison with other large river systems, the vast storage capacity of these lakes causes an unusual stability in the system, reducing fluctuations in level and eliminating floods in the main river, and makes possible some sound measure of control over lake levels. But I agree that any plan to accomplish this purpose must be long range, and any overall plan would require some years to be fully effective.
An examination of the United States lake survey record of monthly mean stages of the great lakes, which extends back over a continuous period of 91 years, reveals that the extreme range in stage experienced by any of the lakes during this period is 6-33 feet, and that occurred in lakes Michigan-Huron. The range experienced by the other lakes during the same period is 4-07 feet in lake Superior, 5-08 feet in lake Erie and 6 29 feet in lake Ontario.
With the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, I would like to place on record a graph of water levels on the great lakes, prepared by the corps of U.S. army engineers, and recording the fluctuations in water levels over a period of 91 years, up to and including
1951.	I believe this graph material would be of immeasurable value to members of this House of Commons who, like myself, are concerned with this problem.

By doing this we would no longer face the terrific losses we now experience or the danger of even greater losses in the future.

As to the liquor, I think you had better carry your own, as far as I can see; and I am still able to carry it.
The point I wanted to make is this. The DC-3's, the other aircraft flying out from Montreal, provide a meal service and there is a considerable contrast between the meal service provided in the North Stars and that provided in the DC-3's. Quite a number of people will continue to use the DC-3's because of the number of flights per day from Montreal. I am referring not only to people who are travelling to Newfoundland but to those who are travelling all over the maritime provinces. From these meals they get a bad impression of the service provided by T.C.A. I am not casting any reflection- nor do I intend to do so-on the personnel of T.C.A. in any way. I do not think you can better the personnel, but I think you can better the meals considerably on the DC-3's, trans-Canada. I have had that complaint made to me by outsiders; and when I speak of outsiders I mean Americans and tourists. I think we should make every effort to try to have meals that compare with the meals provided by American air lines and by our own North Star. I say that not in any carping spirit but with the idea of attempting to make constructive criticism. I also understand that there is going to be a new form of silencer applied to the North Star, or a new muffler system. I think that would be a great help indeed. At the present time the noise is practically deafening and except for the fact that the service is so fast that one puts up with it, really you would not take it from choice. I pass that suggestion along in the spirit merely of constructive criticism.
One other point that I think might be borne in mind is from the point of view of people who may be nervous when travelling in aircraft. If it could be provided in some way or another that these flaming exhausts would not be stuck up in the passengers' faces, I think that might be a good idea as well.
Going from aircraft to landing fields, may I say that when Queen Juliana arrived at Gander, a desolate picture was painted of her landing and of her quarters at Gander itself.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Colonel McCormick.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Don't get me started on that man McCormick. I believe Your Honour has already called me to order on that subject. If I start on it again, I might go too far.
I was speaking of the time that Queen Juliana arrived at Gander airport and of the description which was broadcast of her arrival and which was publicized in the various newspapers. It gave an extremely bleak impression of the quarters provided for travellers at Gander airport. It is all very well to say that no reflections are cast on the place that gives hospitality in such a case, but there really is a grave reflection. When one has the queen of any foreign country described as being quartered in a room that has no floor covering, that has no toilet arrangements of any kind, and that is small, it is bound to cast a reflection. I therefore say in all sincerity-and remember, I am not putting any blame on the Department of Transport or whatever department is concerned, because that is apparently the way that most airports are run-that there should be set up some quarters that might not be used always, that is, they might not be used by any Tom, Dick or Harry.
It is not every day that you have these special people coming here, and I think there should be some quarters set aside that could be used on such occasions as that. It is not a costly business, but it would make all the difference between getting bad publicity and getting the kind of publicity that Canada deserves. I do not think that the queen said anything about it, but I am quite certain that a great number of other people did. We do not want that to happen again. That is just another angle.
I am sure the minister will now follow me in most things that I say as well as he has in the past. The most important thing that I wish to speak about tonight is this; and again it is something that is almost local, but it is practically international, Mr. Speaker. Unfortunately I did not have the answer given me this afternoon because of the enforced absence of the minister who had to attend a meeting in another part of this building. I refer to the operation of a radio station by the United States air force in Newfoundland. To those of us who live within the radius of that station it is most important to have this particular station continued in operation. The terms of its operation are, I understand, that it may be operated by the United States air force until six months from the time that formal peace has been signed with Germany. It has been in operation from the beginning, from the time when the United States forces first came into Newfoundland, and it has given wonderful service and entertainment to the
The Budget-Mr. Higgins people within its radius. I suppose the chief kick that I have heard is this and I am sure that it has been heard not only by me but by all the members from Newfoundland. It has appeared in all our daily papers; it has been broadcast. I know that I for one was buttonholed very often before coming to Ottawa this time. The real worry that the baseball fans have is that this station broadcasts ball games, and it is the only station that does, and that the people down there, the Newfoundlanders and the Americans, who live off the base are not able to hear those programs.
I do not know where the blame rests. It has been passed to various places. I have heard the department of the Secretary of State for External Affairs blamed, but this morning in the committee he disavowed any such blame. As I understand it, it is not the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I have not had an answer from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), but I expect the answer will be that it is not his doing. Where the blame rests I do not know. If the facts are as we have had them outlined in many letters in the Newfoundland press and by many private individuals, the blame would appear to attach to the proprietors of a recently incorporated company that operates a broadcasting station. Unfortunately that broadcasting station-and I do say this, I suppose, in a spirit of criticism-is not unfavourably inclined to my hon. friends opposite. Protests were made before the licence was granted to this particular station. At the time it made its request to be given the right to operate, it stated very definitely that there was lots of room for another station in Newfoundland. As a result of that appeal they were given the right to operate.
Now, I understand-and I understand on authority that I am satisfied is reliable-that one of the proprietors of that particular station, the chief proprietor, went to the American general commanding and told him that his station was not able to stand the competition of the American station, and by other and divers means, whether there were threats or not, Mr. Speaker, I have not been able to ascertain-one does not approach an American general and say, "Tell me the whole story"-but for whatever reason, the station has been put off the air. I do hope very sincerely and honestly, and I am sure my colleagues from Newfoundland will express the same wish-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear, "hear, hear" in agreement. I am sure that the hon. members opposite will also voice the same wish. This station has given us so much pleasure, and

The Budget-Mr. Higgins has given all our people so much pleasure, that whatever steps have to be taken to see to it that the American authorities are reassured that we wish them to continue their broadcasting should be taken. I hope those steps will be taken.
My idea is that they do not wish to offend Canada in any way. It has been suggested to them that by continuing operations as they are they may offend Canada, and for that reason they have stopped. We have to remember-and I am speaking now in the broad sense-that in so far as the United States forces in Newfoundland are concerned, they are possibly the largest industry in the matter of getting money to our people. We must recognize it as the very first great industry we have.
Speakers from Newfoundland on the other side of the house, not only the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick), have enlarged on this particular matter recently. I would not like anything at all to take away the good feelings that exist at the present time between our American friends and the people of Newfoundland. This may very well do so, because, as I say, there are a considerable number of American personnel and tneir families living off the United States base, and they cannot get these programs. Moreover, the base at Argentia is also dependent on the programs coming from Pepperrell

air force base as well. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I do hope that whatever minister is concerned, whether it is the Minister of Transport, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson)-I would even ask the Prime Minister himself (Mr. St. Laurent)-will take a hand in this particular matter because it goes a little further than that. It means good relationship between the newest part of this dominion and our great sister country on the other side of the border. It means very much more than just merely asking that Newfoundlanders will hear the ball games; I can assure you of that.
On motion of Mr. Higgins the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we will proceed with the debate on the budget on Wednesday and Thursday, but tomorrow we will first take up the resolution of the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) to set up a special committee to consider the operations of the national film board. I think that is about all.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
